column4: 2 Checklist 2 (integer arithmetic on input checked); Book ch. 9 (no panics on bad input); the module's own contract (bytes.rs:3-4)
column6: FileSource::raw_read computes `offset + len as u64` (lines 80, 82) without a check, and OffsetSource::read_at computes `self.start + offset` (line 138) the same way, so an offset from disk data near u64::MAX overflows.
column7: Take a primary GPT header with a valid header CRC and entries_lba = 0x007F_FFFF_FFFF_FFFF on a 512-byte-sector disk, with 128 entries of 128 bytes. parttable.rs:222's checked_mul passes 2^64-512 to read_exact_at. In a debug build (the tests) this panics at bytes.rs:80 with 'attempt to add with overflow'. In a release build (profile.release sets no overflow-checks) `end` becomes `size` and `end - start` wraps to size+4096, so raw_read_exact runs `vec![0u8; size+4096]`. On a whole disk larger than RAM plus swap (any multi-TB disk) the allocation fails and `dump` aborts. OffsetSource has the same overflow when `start` comes from a disklabel64 offset (other/dfly.rs:104).
column8: In raw_read: `let Some(stop) = offset.checked_add(len as u64) else { return Vec::new() };`, and return empty when size > 0 and offset >= size. Use stop in place of both `offset + len`. In OffsetSource: `let Some(at) = self.start.checked_add(offset) else { return Vec::new() };`. Test: FileSource and OffsetSource read_at(u64::MAX - 512, 16384) return an empty Vec (the test is named file_source_reads_near_u64_max).
column9: confirmed: I read the code at c4917fc and the failure case holds. bytes.rs:80 computes `self.size.max(offset + len as u64)` without a check. parttable.rs read_entries passes `h.entries_lba.checked_mul(ss)` straight to read_exact_at, and nothing checks that entries_lba < total; read_gpt calls header_valid on the primary before any bounds check. So an offset of 2^64-512 with len 16384 does reach raw_read. Debug build: 'attempt to add with overflow' at line 80. Release build (profile.release sets only lto and strip, so overflow checks are off): - offset+len wraps to 15872. - `end` saturates to u64::MAX, then min(size) gives size. - start is 2^64-4096, so end-start wraps to size+4096. - raw_read_exact then runs vec![0u8; size+4096]. On a disk bigger than RAM plus swap that allocation fails and the process aborts. - On a smaller disk the zeroed allocation succeeds lazily, pread fails with EINVAL, and the result comes back empty. The input needs a GPT header with a valid CRC, which is easy to craft. A disk holt inspects is untrusted input, and bytes.rs:3-4 promises no panics on on-disk data. That fits S1: a panic or abort on real input. The OffsetSource line 138 sub-claim is weaker. In dfly.rs:104, `f.start + base + p.offset_kib * 1024`, and the `offset * block / 1024` at line 59, would overflow before bytes.rs does. Line 138 still has the same unchecked add, though. None of our rules wins: the fix needs no dependency, works on Rust 1.85, and changes no output for valid disks.

column4: 3 Checklist 3; std::process::Child::kill docs (it signals only the child); the type's own doc at sys.rs:41-44 ('a hung zpool must not hang the dump')
column6: The timeout in RealRunner::exec_status does not bound the call: after kill(), child.wait() (line 121) blocks on a process SIGKILL can't reach yet, and reader.join() (line 126) blocks while any grandchild still holds the stdout pipe.
column7: `RealRunner { timeout: 200ms }.run("sh", &["-c", "sleep 30 & echo x"])` returns only after 30 s: sh exits 0, but the background sleep holds the pipe and read_to_end waits for it. A zpool or zfs stuck in uninterruptible sleep on a suspended pool ignores SIGKILL until its I/O returns, so wait() hangs the dump indefinitely. That is the hang the timeout exists for.
column8: After the deadline, kill, then poll try_wait for a short grace period and return None without a blocking wait (leave the child). Have the reader thread send its buffer over an mpsc channel and use recv_timeout in place of join. Optionally spawn with CommandExt::process_group(0) (std 1.64) and signal the group through a hand-declared `extern "C" fn kill`, the same way geteuid is declared. Test: the sh background case above finishes in under 5 s.
column9: confirmed: sys.rs at c4917fc: on the deadline the loop calls child.kill() and then a blocking child.wait(), and after the loop reader.join() waits for read_to_end, which needs EOF from every holder of the stdout pipe. A process in uninterruptible sleep (a zfs/zpool on a suspended pool) blocks wait(), and an inherited pipe keeps join() waiting even after sh exits 0 (try_wait returns Some at once, so the timeout never applies). That defeats the bound the doc at lines 41-44 promises. No holt rule is involved, because the fix needs only std and a hand-declared extern. S2 is the right severity for error handling.

column4: 4 Checklist 4/6 (API shape, duplicated logic); API Guidelines C-COMMON-TRAITS (PartialEq should mean equal values)
column6: Value derives PartialEq, so Int(n) != UInt(n) for the same n >= 0. parse() returns UInt for every non-negative integer, while probes build Int for non-negative values (probe/zfs.rs:316 for uint8/uint16, load/reformat.rs:580 for passno). Equal numbers then compare unequal, and readback.rs:93 `same()` works around this by hand.
column7: `json::parse("5").unwrap() == Value::from(5i32)` is false. Comparing a dumped field read back from the layout file with a freshly probed one by == reports a difference where none exists, unless the caller goes through as_u64 the way readback's same() does.
column8: Write PartialEq by hand so Int and UInt compare by numeric value (or make From<i8..i64> return UInt for n >= 0), then remove readback::same's special case. Printing is identical either way. Check each `==` on Values that load uses, because one that never matched before could now match. Test: assert_eq!(parse("5").unwrap(), Value::from(5i32)).
column9: confirmed: Value derives PartialEq with separate Int(i64) and UInt(u64). parse() returns UInt for any non-negative integer, from_int! maps i8..i64 to Int, probe/zfs.rs:316 builds Int for uint8/uint16, and reformat.rs:580 builds Int for passno. readback.rs:93 same() works around the mismatch through as_u64. I found no live == at c4917fc that misfires today, so this is API shape and duplicated logic (S2), not a wrong result. The fix doesn't change output.

column4: 2 Checklist 2 (file names and arguments as input); RA4 H6 focus (one quoting function, load/mod.rs:507 shell_quote)
column6: bios_grub_pick writes the load target `t` into sh unquoted, both in the for-list and in the `${d#{t}}` pattern. load/mod.rs:331 accepts any absolute --target, so a target with a space or a glob character breaks NixOS's BIOS GRUB step.
column7: With `bko-holt load --target "/mnt/new root"` the command reads `for d in /mnt/new root/nix/store/*-grub-2.*/lib/grub/i386-pc`. The word is split, g ends up empty and the step fails with 'no BIOS GRUB in the Nix store' (exit 1). A target containing `*` or `$(...)` is expanded by the shell. The value is the operator's own argument, not hostile, so this is S2 rather than a quoting hole. The caller at commands.rs:3617 (`chroot {t}`) is H6's.
column8: Quote with crate::load::shell_quote: `T=<quoted t>; for d in "$T"{st}/*-grub-2.*/lib/grub/i386-pc; ... ${d#"$T"}`. Alternatively, have load reject targets that shell_quote would need to quote. shell_quote leaves /mnt/bko-target bare, so golden plans don't change. Test: bios_grub_pick("/mnt/a b") run under sh against a fake store finds the GRUB.
column9: confirmed: bios_grub_pick puts `t` bare into the for-list and into `${d#{t}}`. load/mod.rs:331 checks only that the target starts with '/' and isn't '/'. A target with a space splits into separate words, g comes out empty, and the step exits with 'no BIOS GRUB'. The value is the operator's own --target, not untrusted input, so S2 rather than an S1 quoting hole is fair. The caller commands.rs:3617 (`chroot {t}`) has the same gap, which is H6's. shell_quote leaves /mnt/bko-target unquoted, so golden plans don't change.

column4: 2 Checklist 2; Rustonomicon/std (stack overflow aborts and can't be caught); json.rs:351 MAX_DEPTH as the crate's own precedent
column6: The S-expression reader recurses without a depth limit (datum -> items -> datum, and skip_space's `#;` -> datum), unlike the JSON reader's MAX_DEPTH. It reads files from the dumped root.
column7: If /var/guix/profiles/system-N-link/parameters or the profile manifest on the dumped system holds about 1,000,000 '(' characters, parse_sexps overflows the main thread's stack and `dump` dies with SIGSEGV. Guix never writes such a file; a crafted or damaged one does.
column8: Add a depth field to Reader. Increment it in datum for a list, vector or #vu8, and in the `#;` branch. Past 256, return None, which ends the read the way the doc already describes. Test: parse_sexps(&"(".repeat(1 << 20)) is empty and doesn't crash.
column9: confirmed: Reader::datum -> items -> datum recurses with no depth counter. The quote forms and skip_space's `#;` branch also recurse. json.rs has MAX_DEPTH=256 at line 351, which the sexp reader lacks. guix_json reads the parameters and profile manifest from the dumped root, so a deeply nested file would overflow the stack and abort dump. Guix never writes such a file, so only crafted or damaged input triggers it: S2, not S1.

column4: 7 Checklist 7 (doc against code) and 2; RFC 4648 section 4 (padding and length)
column6: unbase64's doc says 'None on anything else', but the function stops at the first '=' and ignores whatever follows, keeps a dangling 6-bit group, and accepts lengths that aren't a multiple of 4. Its result goes to disk through load/writetable.rs:73, 176, 183 and 189.
column7: unbase64("QlRY=QlRY") returns Some(b"BTX") and unbase64("Q") returns Some([]). A layout whose code_b64, gap_b64 or esp_image b64 was cut or edited decodes to a shorter blob without any error, and load writes that blob as boot code or as the ESP image.
column8: After removing whitespace, require len % 4 == 0, allow '=' only as the last one or two characters, and require the spare bits to be zero. Return None otherwise. Tests: "QlRY=QlRY", "Q" and "QQ=" are None.
column9: downgraded: The facts hold: unbase64 breaks at the first '=', drops a dangling 6-bit group, and doesn't check the length, so "QlRY=QlRY" gives BTX and "Q" gives an empty vec, against a doc that says 'None on anything else'. But the proposed fix doesn't produce the error the finding wants. Every writetable caller already discards a None: code_b64 goes through .unwrap_or_default(), gap_b64 and image_b64 through .and_then(...).filter(...) so the write is skipped, and esp_image through `else { continue }`. A strict decoder turns a silently short blob into a silently missing one, which is the same broken boot either way. The input is a hand-edited or corrupted layout, not real dump output. What remains is a doc-against-code mismatch (S3). Making callers report an error would change exit codes, so under rule 5 that goes to the user.

column4: 2 Checklist 2 (wrong result on real input); mdadm.conf(5) (DEVICE lines may repeat and accumulate)
column6: parse_mdadm_conf keys every keyword other than ARRAY with Obj::put, which replaces an earlier value. A second DEVICE (or MAILADDR, CREATE, ...) line therefore drops the first from the report.
column7: With `DEVICE /dev/sd*` followed by `DEVICE /dev/nvme*`, settings.device is "/dev/nvme*" alone. The dump misreports the configuration. Only the report reads it (report.rs:1586), not load.
column8: Join a repeated keyword's words with a space, or make settings.<kw> an array when the keyword repeats. This changes dump JSON, so under rule 5 it goes to the user. Test: two DEVICE lines both appear.
column9: confirmed: Obj::put (json.rs:176) replaces the value of an existing key. parse_mdadm_conf calls other.put(kw.to_ascii_lowercase(), ...) for each non-ARRAY line, so a second DEVICE line overwrites the first. mdadm.conf(5) allows DEVICE lines to repeat and accumulate. Only report.rs:1586/1633 consumes it. No load code reads mdadm_conf at c4917fc, so the damage is a misreported report field (S2). The fix changes dump JSON, so under rule 5 it goes to the user rather than into a cleanup commit. That routes the fix; it doesn't refute the finding.

column4: 1 Checklist 1/7 (FFI layouts proved against headers; comments not stale)
column6: I checked the statvfs struct against both C libraries and it is correct on every cfg that compiles it. Only the comments are wrong: line 356 and the SAFETY comment at 377-378 say 'glibc's' although the musl targets compile the same code. Sys::statvfs's doc (line 302) doesn't say it returns None off 64-bit Linux.
column7: No failure; this is a documentation fix only.
column8: Have the comment name both headers: glibc sysdeps/unix/sysv/linux/bits/statvfs.h, where __f_unused exists only when __WORDSIZE == 32; and musl include/sys/statvfs.h, where fsblkcnt_t and fsfilcnt_t are unsigned _Int64 and the unnamed bitfield is 8*(2*sizeof(int)-sizeof(long)) = 0 on LP64. On x86_64 and aarch64 (and big-endian 64-bit) both libraries give 112 bytes: 11 x 8-byte fields, then f_type plus 5 ints, which our [c_int; 6] matches in size. f_frsize is at offset 8, f_blocks at 16, f_bfree at 24, f_bavail at 32, all equal to ours. Add '# None' wording to Sys::statvfs.

column6: ParseError implements neither Display nor std::error::Error. Callers format e.message by hand, for example bugreport.rs:520.
column8: impl Display ("{message} at byte {offset}") and Error for ParseError. Keep the callers' current message text so output doesn't change.

column4: 2 clippy-parser restriction set (arithmetic_side_effects, indexing_slicing, cast_possible_truncation)
column6: Parser-lint hits in the unit: arithmetic_side_effects 19 and indexing_slicing 15 (all in bytes.rs), cast_possible_truncation 12 (bytes 8, blockdev 1, mounts 1, testutil 2). Apart from the S1 hits (bytes.rs:80, 82 and 138) I read each one and found it bounded: CRC index masked with & 0xff, base64 index masked with & 63, SHA-256 on fixed 64-word arrays, slices taken after a length check, and a mounts octal value of at most 0o777 checked against 0xff. blockdev.rs:176 `size * 512` and :178 `n as u32` operate on sysfs values the kernel keeps small (bdev size fits in loff_t, so it can't overflow).
column8: Write blockdev.rs:176 as checked_mul(512).unwrap_or(0) and :178 as u32::try_from(n).ok() for the record. Elsewhere, add `#[allow]` with a one-line proof once RA3's policy says how.

column6: Two unwraps rely on invariants that are true but stated nowhere: json.rs:558 from_utf8 of bytes the number scanner has accepted (ASCII only), and bytes.rs:152 try_into on a slice that is exactly N bytes long.

column4: 4 API Guidelines C-CUSTOM-TYPE, C-CONV; checklist 4 (bool parameters)
column6: Several API shapes fall short of the guidelines. Sys::new takes a bare bool `privileged`, so call sites read `Sys::new(root, runner, true)`. Sys::statvfs returns an anonymous (u64, u64, u64). store::parse_manifest returns (String, String, String, String). blockdev::Kind::name would conventionally be as_str/Display. RealRunner, FakeRunner and Sys.privileged have pub fields.
column8: Add a small Usage {size, free, avail} struct and a ManifestEntry struct, rename name to as_str and implement Display, and consider an enum or a named constructor for privilege. Output doesn't change.

column4: 7 Checklist 7 (doc against code)
column6: Two json docs don't match the code. pretty()'s doc says scalar arrays 'that fit on one line' stay inline, but the test at line 264 measures the compact form without the ', ' spaces and without the key, so lines past 100 columns occur. parse() keeps duplicate object keys and get() returns the first one; neither is documented, and the parser reads LUKS2's JSON area.
column8: Fix only the docs. Changing the layout would change output (rule 5).

column4: 2 Book ch. 9 / C-GOOD-ERR (panic only for bugs, never for bad input); ByteSource's own contract at bytes.rs:16 ("fewer at the end")
column6: FileSource::raw_read adds offset + len unchecked. For an offset within len of u64::MAX the release build wraps, `end - start` (line 82) underflows to about the device size, and raw_read_exact then allocates that many bytes; the debug build panics. The parsers in this unit pass such offsets straight from disk bytes (H1's file, but only H2's parsers reach it).
column7: A 2 TiB partition carries an LVM label (LABELONE + "LVM2 001") whose first metadata-area entry reads FF FF FF FF FF FF FF FF. holt checks neither the label CRC nor the mda checksum. probe/lvm.rs:48/66 passes off = u64::MAX to read_metadata, and lvm.rs:98 calls read_exact_at(u64::MAX, 512) -> FileSource::read_at -> raw_read. There start = 0xFFFF_FFFF_FFFF_F000, offset+len wraps to 511, end = size = 2^41, and end - start wraps to 2^41 + 4096. `vec![0u8; 2 TiB + 4 KiB]` fails and `bko-holt dump` aborts with "memory allocation of 2199023259648 bytes failed" (I simulated this arithmetic with u64 wrapping; I could not run it, as the Mac has no Rust toolchain). Other reachers: bootcode.rs:63 (GRUB kernel sector lba with lba*ss in [2^64-512, 2^64), no checksum on boot code) and parttable.rs:222 (entries_lba*ss, gated by the header CRC). No test catches it: every probe test reads a MemSource, which handles any offset.
column8: In raw_read, return Vec::new() when offset >= self.size or when offset.checked_add(len as u64) is None, then compute end from the checked sum. MemSource and OffsetSource already behave this way. Test: FileSource over a small temp file, read_at(u64::MAX, 512) and read_at(u64::MAX - 100, 16384) return empty; and lvm::probe on a FileSource-backed PV image whose mda offset is u64::MAX returns metadata_error.
column9: confirmed: Confirmed from c4917fc. probe/lvm.rs takes each metadata-area offset straight from the PV header with no bound or checksum and calls read_metadata, and lvm.rs:98 calls src.read_exact_at(off, 512). For a FileSource, read_at skips the head cache, because u64::MAX.saturating_add(512) is greater than HEAD, so the read goes to raw_read. There start = u64::MAX - 4095 = 0xFFFF_FFFF_FFFF_F000. The saturating chain gives u64::MAX, but the min() argument uses an unchecked `offset + len as u64`. Cargo.toml's [profile.release] sets only lto and strip, so overflow checks are off in release, the sum wraps to 511 and max(size, 511) = size. That makes end = size, and `end - start` wraps to size + 4096. raw_read_exact then runs vec![0u8; ~2 TiB + 4 KiB]. Under Linux's default heuristic overcommit, a zeroed allocation larger than RAM plus swap is refused, so the process aborts through handle_alloc_error. With overcommit set to always, the allocation succeeds and pread at an offset above i64::MAX fails with EINVAL, so it returns empty, but that is not the default. A debug build panics on the add at line 80. MemSource and OffsetSource both return empty for out-of-range offsets, so the probe tests never see this. The rust-audit.md S1 definition includes 'a panic or wrong result on real input', and the doc names holt's parsers of damaged disks as a top risk. An abort of `bko-holt dump` on a corrupt or hostile PV header fits that definition, so S1 stands. No rule wins: the fix needs no dependency or newer Rust, and it changes no output on valid input. A corrupt header would produce metadata_error instead of an abort. One correction to the finding: parttable.rs:222 is reachable only through a CRC-valid GPT header, and the bootcode.rs reacher multiplies lba by ss with checked_mul first, so it is reachable only when the product lands within 512 bytes of u64::MAX. Both are narrower than the LVM path, but they do not change the verdict.

column4: 2 Book ch. 9 (no crash on bad input); the crate's own precedent: section_body caps depth at 64 (lvm.rs:216), json.rs MAX_DEPTH 256, zfs.rs MAX_DEPTH 32
column6: value() recurses on every '[' with no depth bound. section_body limits section nesting, but array nesting escapes it, and metadata text up to MAX_METADATA (16 MiB) is parsed, unchecksummed, straight from the disk. I graded it S2 because it needs constructed text, not random damage; argue S1 if hostile disks are in scope.
column7: A PV whose metadata area holds `vg { id = "x" seqno = 1 a = ` followed by 1,000,000 '[' passes read_metadata. tokenize makes 1M Punct tokens, and value() recurses 1M frames deep. Result: "thread 'main' has overflowed its stack", SIGABRT, and bko-holt dump dies on that disk. Along the way tokenize holds the text as Vec<char> plus Vec<Tok>: several hundred MiB for 16 MiB of punctuation.
column8: Thread a depth argument through value() (from section_body's depth) and return Err("nested too deeply") past the same limit. LVM writes arrays one level deep, so real metadata is unaffected. Test: in config_syntax, assert parse_config(&("a = ".to_string() + &"[".repeat(100_000))).is_err().
column9: confirmed: At c4917fc, value() in lvm.rs recurses on every Tok::Punct('[') and has no depth argument. section_body's `depth > 64` check only counts '{' sections, and the config_syntax test only checks section nesting ('a { ' x100). read_metadata checks only the magic, the flags and the bounds (loc_size <= 16 MiB), with no CRC on the text, so `a = ` followed by deeply nested '[' reaches parse_config. About 1M frames overflows any default stack and aborts the dump, where every other bad input gets an Err in metadata_error. The memory estimate holds: 16M chars as Vec<char> is 64 MiB, and Vec<Tok> at about 32 bytes per token is about 512 MiB. The text has to be built on purpose, and these are the user's own disks, so S2 rather than S1. No rule wins: the fix adds no dependency and changes no output for real metadata.

column4: 2 clippy::arithmetic_side_effects (restriction, RA3 parser-module policy); Book ch. 9
column6: There are 154 arithmetic_side_effects hits in the unit. Nearly all are bounded. The ones that can overflow multiply a raw disk or metadata field: md.rs:56 (super_offset*512 inside the validation guard) and 82-86; ext.rs:147 (blocks*block_size, blocks 64-bit); xfs.rs:87; f2fs.rs:59; bfs.rs:19; misc.rs:83 (JFS); lvm.rs:291, 292, 306 (+=), 316, 335; parttable.rs:342, 371 (backup_lba+1), 421, 427, 428; luks.rs:110 (key_size*8); luksheader.rs:64. They panic in debug builds and wrap silently in release. fat.rs:165 already uses saturating_mul, so the unit is inconsistent.
column7: Only absurd values reach it. In release, wrapping in md.rs:56 lets a superblock whose super_offset is off/512 + 2^55 pass the stale-copy check. In debug (cargo test, a D9 harness), an ext superblock with the 64bit flag and blocks_hi = 0xFFFFFFFF panics at ext.rs:147. Report sizes wrap to small numbers instead of being refused or saturated.
column8: Use checked_mul in the md.rs:56 guard (treat None as a mismatch). Use saturating_mul or saturating_add for reported byte sizes, as fat.rs:165 does. Use checked arithmetic in luksheader::hdr_and_areas, with an overflow meaning not whole.

column4: 2 rustdoc book / RFC 1574 (# Panics); C-GOOD-ERR; Effective Rust (std over hand-rolled, within rule 1)
column6: csum is `pub`, takes any slice, and reads up to 256 + 2*max_dev bytes through a local panicking le32 (mdsb.rs:15, which shadows crate::bytes::le32's non-panicking one). Only set_logical_block_size's check at line 44 keeps it in bounds. That precondition is undocumented, with no # Panics.
column7: A caller handing csum the 4096-byte superblock of a member whose max_dev field is >= 1921 (damaged, or another format's data with the md magic) panics with an index out of bounds at mdsb.rs:16. Today only set_logical_block_size and the test call it, so it is latent.
column8: Make csum private, or have it return Option<u32> after checking 256 + 2*max_dev <= sb.len(). Use crate::bytes::le32/le16 and drop the local helper. Add # Errors to set_logical_block_size (clippy missing_errors_doc at mdsb.rs:37).
column9: confirmed: mdsb::csum is pub in the bko_holt lib crate and takes any &[u8]. Its local le32 indexes b[o..o+3] directly (mdsb.rs:15-17), and crate::bytes::le32 returns 0 out of range instead. Its loop reads 256 + 2*max_dev bytes, so max_dev >= 1921 runs past 4096 and panics. A slice shorter than 224 bytes panics too. Only set_logical_block_size's check at line 44 guards it, and nothing documents that precondition. The panic comes from indexing, which clippy's missing_panics_doc does not flag, so this is API shape, not lint-nameable polish. It is latent, since all callers are guarded today, which keeps it at S2. No rule wins.

column4: 2 checklist 2 (casts on input via try_from); clippy::cast_possible_truncation; C-GOOD-ERR
column6: from_json reads the layout JSON's GELI fields with truncating `as` casts: version `as u32` (157), ealgo_id/aalgo_id `as u16` (163-164), keylen `as u16` (170), sectorsize `as u32` (173), iterations `as i32` (175). An out-of-range value silently becomes a different, valid-looking parameter for geli init instead of being refused.
column7: In a layout record (hand-edited or damaged), "keylen": 65792 gives Meta.keylen 256. "sectorsize": 4294971392 gives 4096. "ealgo_id": 65558 gives 22 (AES-XTS). "iterations": 4294967295 gives -1, which other/geli.rs:467/580 read as no `-i`. load then runs geli init with parameters the record never had.
column8: Use u16::try_from / u32::try_from / i32::try_from(...).ok()? so an out-of-range record yields None, which other/geli.rs:329 already handles. In-range values are unchanged. Test: from_json on the guest content with keylen 65792 is None.
column9: confirmed: from_json does what the finding says: `x.as_u64()? as u32` for version, `n("ealgo_id").map(|x| x as u16)` and the same for aalgo_id, `n("keylen")? as u16`, `n("sectorsize")? as u32`, and `as_i64().unwrap_or(-1) as i32` for iterations. 65792 as u16 is 256, and 4294967295 as i32 is -1, which the init and setkey paths (`m.iterations >= 0`) read as no -i. A record that dump writes from a real sector is always in range (u16/u32 on disk), so only hand-edited or damaged layout JSON triggers it: S2, not S1. When from_json returns None, providers() at other/geli.rs:329 falls back to the content record and otherwise keeps meta None, which load already handles. The fix changes behaviour only for out-of-range input, so under rule 5 it goes to the user rather than into a cleanup commit. That decides how it is fixed, not whether the finding stands.

column4: 2 checklist 2 (wrong result on real input); Linux include/linux/kdev_t.h new_decode_dev (from memory, not re-read here)
column6: journal_device decodes s_journal_dev as (dev>>8)&0xfff : dev&0xff. That drops the minor's high bits 20-31, which new_decode_dev (as ext4 uses it, and as e2fsprogs stores st_rdev) puts back. Any external journal on a device with minor >= 256 is reported under the wrong device. By the letter this is S1; I filed S2 because only the report shows it: nothing in holt/src reads journal_device.
column7: An ext4 filesystem with its external journal on /dev/loop300 (7:300) has s_journal_dev = 0x10072C, and the report prints "journal_device": "7:44".
column8: minor = (dev & 0xff) | ((dev >> 12) & 0xfff00), major = (dev >> 8) & 0xfff. Test: a sample with s_journal_dev 0x10072C reports "7:300".
column9: confirmed: ext.rs:200 formats journal_dev as `(dev>>8)&0xfff : dev&0xff`, which drops the minor's bits from (dev>>12)&0xfff00. Linux new_decode_dev puts those bits back, ext4 decodes s_journal_dev that way, and mke2fs stores st_rdev, whose low 32 bits use the same encoding. 7:300 encodes to 0x10072C, and the current code prints 7:44, as the finding says. git grep finds journal_device nowhere in the repo except ext.rs itself and its 8:17 test, so only the report shows it, and minors >= 256 for an external journal are rare. S2 rather than S1 is fair. The fix changes JSON output, so under rule 5 it goes to the user; that sets the route, it is not a rule-wins drop.

column4: 2 checklist 2 (wrong result from input); Book ch. 9
column6: Ctx::resolve splits the spec at its first '=' before checking for a /dev/ path, so a device path that contains '=' (a udev by-label/by-partlabel link) never resolves.
column7: An ext4 labelled `data=1`, fstab line `/dev/disk/by-label/data=1 /data ext4 defaults` (udev keeps '=' in link names: systemd's whitelisted_char_for_devnode allows "#+-.:=@_", from memory, not checked on a host). split_once gives key `/dev/disk/by-label/data`, val `1`, so the match falls to `_ => None` and storage.fstab[].resolves_to is null. load's mount stage (load/commands.rs ~3011) then logs "fstab's /data (ext4) isn't on the layout's disks; not mounted", and restore writes /data's files into the root filesystem while the restored /data filesystem stays empty.
column8: Take the `/dev/` branch first: `if spec.starts_with('/') { ...canonicalize... }` and only then `split_once('=')` for the UUID/LABEL/PARTUUID/PARTLABEL tags. Test: a resolve unit test on a Tree with /dev/disk/by-label/data=1 linking to a partition, and an fstab scenario asserting resolves_to.
column9: confirmed: At c4917fc, Ctx::resolve (holt/src/report.rs:224-255) runs `spec.split_once('=')` before anything else. The bare-path branch only fires when key is "", so `/dev/disk/by-label/data=1` gives key `/dev/disk/by-label/data`, which hits `_ => None`. The canonicalize step and the fallback that matches udev links are never reached. The fstab JSON (report.rs:1477) takes resolves_to straight from resolve with no fallback to the device or mountpoint. load's mount stage (load/commands.rs:3010-3019) skips any entry whose resolves_to is null, except a legacy ZFS one, and notes "isn't on the layout's disks; not mounted". So the restore writes into the unmounted mountpoint directory on the root filesystem. udev and blkid encoding keep '=' in link names (whitelist "#+-.:=@_"; I recalled this, I did not check it on a host), so the input is legal, though rare. The same split hits crypttab devices and mount sources too (mounts_of tries devno first). It's a wrong result on real input, so S1 holds. Rule 5 doesn't win, because this is a bug fix and the finding already marks it changes_output for the user. The suggested fix (check the bare /dev/ path first, then split for the tags) is sound, since LABEL=a=b already splits correctly at the first '='.

column6: parse_zfs_get splits `zfs get -H` lines with splitn(4, '\t') from the left, so a tab inside a property value moves part of the value into `source`; the same left-split is used for `zpool get` (515-527) and for `zfs list` columns (566).
column7: `zfs set org:note=$'a\tb' rpool/home` makes `zfs get -H -o name,property,value,source` print `rpool/home\torg:note\ta\tb\tlocal`; parse_zfs_get returns value `a`, source `b\tlocal`, so the dump's properties (what load's `zfs create -o` uses) record a truncated value with a source that is neither local nor received. The unit test at 1761 asserts the opposite assumption ("A tab in the value isn't possible"); I found no character check on user-property values in libzfs from memory, so this is UNVERIFIED against a running zfs.
column8: Names and property names can't hold a tab: take name and property with splitn(3) from the left and the source with rsplit_once('\t') from the right, the rest is the value. For zpool get the same (property left, source right). For `zfs list` columns, put any free-text column (mountpoint, user properties) last or read them with `zfs get` instead. Test: extend zfs_get_lines with a value containing a tab.
column9: confirmed: report.rs:598-604 uses splitn(4,'\t') from the left, so any tab in a value moves into source. The test at 1756-1762 feeds exactly that line ('rpool\tdesc\ta\tb c\tlocal') and asserts the wrong split is intended. zpool get (515-527) does split('\t') and reads f[2] as the source, so with a tab in a pool user property value the 'local' check fails and local_properties drops the property. The props feed load's zfs create -o. Whether OpenZFS accepts a tab in a user property value can't be proven from our code; libzfs checks only the name and length, so I take it as possible. The input is contrived, so S2 and not S1. The fix changes output (rule 5), so it goes to the user.

column4: 2 Book ch. 9 / checklist 2: wrong result on real input
column6: detect_loader_on names any BootCurrent path containing SHIM as GRUB before it checks for REFIND. As a result, rEFInd booted through shim is reported as grub, and load's own refusal for `("refind", true) if via_shim` (load/commands.rs:3778) can't be reached through the BootCurrent path.
column7: uefi, current_file `\EFI\refind\shimx64.efi` (refind-install --shim's layout: shim in EFI/refind, rEFInd renamed grubx64.efi beside refind.conf), no LoaderInfo (rEFInd sets none), packages refind + shim-signed + grub-efi-amd64-signed (Ubuntu's default). Result: name=grub, via_shim=true, package=grub-efi-amd64-signed. The loader match at commands.rs:3546 then takes GRUB's path on a machine that boots rEFInd, instead of the rEFInd-through-shim problem. The file layout is from the rEFInd docs (refind-install --shim) and was not checked against a guest; the code path itself is verified.
column8: In the current_file branch, when u contains SHIM set shim = true and choose the name from the directory: `\EFI\REFIND\` gives refind (and LIMINE gives limine), otherwise grub as today. Or check REFIND/LIMINE before the generic SHIM test and set shim from SHIM separately. Test: loader_other_cases with current_file `\EFI\refind\shimx64.efi`, esp_files EFI/refind/grubx64.efi + EFI/refind/refind.conf, expecting name refind and via_shim true.
column9: confirmed: At c4917fc, detect_loader_on (boot.rs:1218-1251) checks `u.contains("SHIM")` before `u.contains("REFIND")`, and that branch sets name=grub. So a BootCurrent of \EFI\refind\shimx64.efi gives name=grub and shim=true. Nothing later fixes this: the LoaderInfo block only fills an empty name (`name.or`) or matches GRUB, systemd-boot or Limine strings, and rEFInd sets no LoaderInfo. The ESP-file fallback only runs when name is None. The package match then picks the arch's grub_efi_packages, so grub-efi-amd64-signed is chosen if it is installed. In load/commands.rs the loader match takes GRUB's arm. The `("refind", true) if via_shim` refusal (around 3778) is never reached from this path, so load reinstalls or points at GRUB on a rEFInd machine instead of stopping with its 'not supported' problem. That is a wrong result on a plausible real layout: refind-install --shim puts shim in EFI/refind and points the NVRAM entry at it. The existing tests only cover \EFI\refind\refind_x64.efi. No rule wins: this is a correctness bug, not a style request. The fix does change the dump's JSON (loader name), so under rule 5 it goes to the user before it is committed, as the finding's changes_output=true already says. The guest layout was not checked, which the finding states itself; the code path is confirmed.

column4: 3 C-GOOD-ERR / checklist 3, 7: silent, order-dependent truncation; doc doesn't state the limits
column6: esp_inventory's 500-file limit is checked only when walk enters a directory, not per file, and hitting it says nothing. One big directory can therefore run far past 500 files, while every directory that sorts after it, and loader/ itself, is left out of the dump without a warning.
column7: An ESP whose EFI/ has a vendor directory that natural-sorts before EFI/debian (for example EFI/HP) with 600 files: walk lists all 600, then returns at entry for EFI/Microsoft, EFI/debian and loader/. boot.esps[].contents.files lacks EFI/debian/grubx64.efi and loader/entries/*. debian_grub_stub is null, and detect_loader's ESP-file fallback (line 1297) misses grub. On Aeon the loop at line 698 is also skipped (files.len() >= 500), so bls_problems (transactional.rs:455-470) would report every entry's linux/initrd as not on the ESP. Whether real ESPs reach 500 files was not checked; the mechanism is verified.
column8: Check the limit per pushed file inside the loop, call sys.warn once when it is hit ("ESP M: more than 500 files; the inventory stops there"), and state the depth-4 and 500-file limits in the doc. Test: an esp_inventory case with Tree EFI/AAA holding 600 files plus EFI/debian/grubx64.efi, asserting the warning and the count.
column9: confirmed: At c4917fc, walk() checks `out.len() >= 500` only when it enters a directory, and its loop pushes every file with no check. sys.list sorts with natural_cmp, which compares bytes, so 'H' (and 'M') sort before 'd': EFI/HP with 600 files is listed in full, and EFI/Microsoft, EFI/debian and the later top-level loader/ then return at once. The entries loop also skips on `files.len() >= 500`. No sys.warn is raised anywhere. The doc comment gives neither the depth-4 nor the 500-file limit. Typical Windows/OEM ESPs (~100-200 files) probably stay under 500, so S2 (silent error handling) rather than S1 is right. The fix adds a warning, an output change, so it goes to the user under rule 5.

column4: 7 checklist 7 (doc against code) / Boot Loader Specification (initrd and options may repeat)
column6: systemd_boot_json's kv() puts each key into an Obj whose put() replaces an earlier key, so a BLS entry with two initrd lines (Arch's microcode image followed by initramfs-linux.img) or several options lines keeps only the last one. The function's doc doesn't say so; only a comment in load (transactional.rs:469) knows.
column7: An entry `linux /vmlinuz-linux`, `initrd /intel-ucode.img`, `initrd /initramfs-linux.img` dumps as initrd "/initramfs-linux.img". The microcode image is in neither the dump nor bls_problems' ESP check.
column8: With no output change: document on systemd_boot_json that a repeated key keeps its last line's value. With an output change, for the user to decide: also emit an `initrds` array when an entry has more than one initrd line, and join repeated options lines with spaces as the spec does. Test: an esp_and_systemd_boot case with two initrd lines.
column9: confirmed: json.rs Obj::put finds an existing key and overwrites its slot, so in kv() a second `initrd` or `options` line replaces the first. Arch's intel-ucode.img + initramfs-linux.img therefore dumps as the last one only. The only acknowledgement is the comment in load/transactional.rs bls_problems: "(The dump keeps one initrd an entry: its last line's.)". systemd_boot_json's doc says nothing. The doc-only fix keeps output unchanged. The array/joined-options variant is an output change for the user, as the finding says.

column4: 6 checklist 5, 6: duplicated logic, needless reads in a loop (Effective Rust)
column6: Is this file a byte copy of one of these? is written three times: esp_inventory's twin search (711-714), same_file (1811-1815) and elilo_json's loader copy (1880). esp_inventory's copy re-reads `path` inside the closure for every same-size candidate.
column7: With k same-size .efi files on an ESP, esp_inventory reads each one (up to 64 MiB) k times instead of once, about 2·k² full-file reads in all. The three copies can also drift apart: only esp_inventory has the 64 MiB cap.
column8: One helper, e.g. `fn byte_copy_of<'a>(sys, path, size, candidates: impl IntoIterator<Item = (&'a str, u64)>) -> Option<&'a str>`, that reads `path` once and filters by size first, used at all three sites with today's candidate order (first match wins) so the output stays the same.
column9: confirmed: esp_inventory's find closure calls sys.read_bytes for `path` again for each same-size candidate (lines 711-714). same_file (1811-1815) reads `path` once and filters by size first. elilo_json (1880) compares every .efi against the in-memory ELILO_EFI bytes with no size filter. Only esp_inventory has the 64 MiB cap. All three answer the same question, so the duplication and the needless reads in a loop are real. The rubric calls duplicated logic S2. The k² cost is small in practice: same-size distinct .efi files are few. The elilo site fits a shared helper less cleanly, since its candidates carry no sizes and its reference is an external file.

column7: The USAGE's own example: run `restic-bko backup ... 2> backup-errors.txt` on a machine whose user bob has no separate /home/bob mount, so bob appears nowhere in the dump. The corpus dumps confirm user names are normally absent: only /home. The file holds `lstat /home/bob/.cache/x: permission denied`. column9: confirmed: At c4917fc, Collector::see_text (redact.rs:379-382) only appends to the corpus and never calls scan(). bugreport.rs passes the text it gathers through see_text alone: load's recorded stderr (352), the logs (406) and the --stderr files (415). The Redactor only rewrites identifiers it has learned, so a /home/USER name or a UUID that appears only in that text goes through r.text() unchanged. The failure case is real: across the corpus dumps, the only /home/USER value is /home/omnios, and the only other user-like strings are Ubuntu's USERDATA/root_ and home_ datasets, which GENERIC_USERS keeps. A `restic-bko backup 2> errs.txt` holding `/home/bob/...` therefore leaks 'bob', against USAGE's promise that every user name gets a pseudonym. leaks() only checks substitutions it already learned, so it can't catch this. A privacy leak on real input is S1 under RA5. No rule wins. Rule 5 only means the fix changes output and goes to the user first (RA7); the finding already says changes_output: true.

That edge requires a non-alphanumeric byte before the '/', so a ZFS dataset name such as rpool/home/bob keeps the name, while its mountpoint /home/bob becomes /home/user1. The report then maps the pseudonym back to the real name for any reader.
column7: A Debian root-on-ZFS system set up as the OpenZFS guide does (`zfs create rpool/home/$username`), or FreeBSD 14+ where adduser makes zroot/home/USER (the debian13-zfs corpus dump already has rpool/home/root in this shape). column6: sfdisk_quote escapes a GPT partition name's `"` and `\` with backslashes. As I recall libfdisk, its script reader has no backslash escapes: a `"` toggles the quote, and only `\xNN` is decoded, which is what `sfdisk --dump` writes. A newline in a name also ends the script line.
column7: (If the recollection holds.) A partition name `a\b` is written as `name="a\\b"`, comes back as `a\\b` (two backslashes), and the restored GPT name differs silently. A name `say "hi"` gives `name="say \"hi\""`, the token ends at the second quote, and sfdisk fails to parse the rest of the line, so the partition stage fails.
column8: Check against util-linux's libfdisk/src/script.c first. If confirmed, write `"`, `\`, `$`, backtick and non-printables as `\xNN`, as fputs_quoted does. Test: sfdisk_script with labels `a\b`, `say "hi"` and `x\ny`, plus a round-trip through `sfdisk --dump` on a loop file in a test guest.
column9: confirmed: Checked against upstream util-linux, which I fetched because no local copy exists. In libfdisk/src/script.c, next_token() has no backslash handling: a `"` toggles open_quote, and a `"` met while inside quotes closes the token, which then has to be followed by a blank, `,` or `;`, or the parse fails. In parse_line_nameval(), name= goes through next_string() and then unhexmangle_string(), which decodes only \xNN. In include/carefulputc.h, fputs_quoted writes `"`, `\`, backtick, `$` and non-printables as \xNN. Holt's sfdisk_quote (402-404) writes `\\` and `\"` instead. So `a\b` comes back from sfdisk as `a\\b`, a silent wrong GPT name. `say "hi"` ends the token at the inner quote, the parse fails and the partition stage fails. A newline is written raw and ends the script line. Partition labels come straight from the dump (layout.rs 136 partlabel) without validation. A silent wrong result on real input, however rare, is S1 under RA5, so I put it one level up. column6: Numbers from the layout JSON (bko-holt's own dump, but it may be hand-edited or rewritten by --fit-largest/--reformat) are used unchecked. `num(md, raid_disks) as usize` sizes a `vec!["missing"; n]` (1308). There are unchecked multiplications and additions: thin_of `extents * ext` (995) and `* 512`, mke2fs `b * n / 1024` (1990), luks_keep_header `offset + size` (1510-1511), btrfs_inside `id + 1` (2671). Release builds have no overflow-checks, so these wrap silently; debug builds panic.
column7: A layout with md raid_disks 4611686018427387904 makes `vec![String; n]` hit capacity overflow, and bko-holt load panics or aborts during plan. A LUKS2 segment with offset 2^64-512 and size 1024 wraps `offset + size` in release, so the 'segment doesn't fit' check passes wrongly.
column8: Cap raid_disks (the md maximum is 1920 for 1.x) and push a problem past it. Use checked_mul/checked_add with a problem on overflow, as thin_of already does with saturating_sub. Test: a thin_refusals-style test with absurd raid_disks, extent_count and LUKS offsets, expecting problems and no panic.
column9: confirmed: md() (1307-1308) does `num(&md, "raid_disks").unwrap_or(0) as usize` and then `vec!["missing".into(); n]` with no cap. A JSON value of 2^62 overflows capacity and panics, and 2^32-1 aborts on allocation. The other sites are unchecked too: `extents * ext` (995), `stripe_size * 512` (986), `b * n / 1024` (1990), `offset + size` (1510-1511, both in the comparison and in the message), and `id + 1` (2671). Cargo.toml's [profile.release] doesn't set overflow-checks, so release builds wrap, and the LUKS check can pass wrongly. The dump's real values are bounded: report.rs parses raid_disks from sysfs as u32, and the kernel and cryptsetup limit the rest. So only hand-edited or corrupt JSON reaches these, not real input, and S2 rather than S1 fits. RA4 item 2 names JSON input explicitly, so the finding stands. The fix adds problems on absurd input only, which is a behaviour change for the user to approve, not rule-wins.

column4: 2 RA4 item 2 (input: file names) and RA5 S1 (a quoting hole, here glob syntax); rustic_core blob/tree/excludes.rs reads --glob-file lines with ignore::overrides::OverrideBuilder, which uses gitignore glob syntax
column6: Plan::globs() writes alias and shared-snapshot backup paths into the restore's --glob-file without escaping glob metacharacters, so a path containing [, ], *, ?, { or \ is read as a pattern and not as a literal path.
column7: A plain btrfs snapshot @/backups/pre[1] of @ mounted at / gives backup path /backups/pre[1] and the glob line !/backups/pre[1]/**. In rustic that matches /backups/pre1/** and does not match the literal /backups/pre[1]. The main restore then fills /backups/pre[1] (which should have been left empty), so the shared-snapshot step that makes the snapshot there finds a non-empty directory. Any real /backups/pre1 is also left out of the restore. The same happens with an alias such as /mnt/top/@data[2024].
column8: Escape \ * ? [ ] { } with a backslash in each path before adding !…/** (one helper, also used for commands.rs's pool, reformat and raw globs). Test: shared.rs plan() with sub "@/backups/pre[1]" asserting globs() == ["!/backups/pre\\[1\\]/**"], and a rustic-bko restore round trip with such a name in the bko corpus.
column9: confirmed: Confirmed from the code. At c4917fc, Plan::globs() (shared.rs:115-118) builds lines with plain format!("!{a}/**") and format!("!{}/**", s.backup), where the paths come verbatim from the layout's subvolume paths through backup_path/aliases/join. Nothing escapes them. commands.rs:3166-3225 writes those lines to restore.globs as they are and passes --glob-file to the archiver, which is rustic-bko (restic has no --glob-file). In rustic_core (branch backotter), crates/core/src/blob/tree/excludes.rs::as_override hands each line to ignore::overrides::OverrideBuilder::add. That uses gitignore glob syntax with backslash escaping on, so [1] is a character class and *, ?, {..} and \ are special. So the exclude line !/backups/pre[1]/** misses the literal /backups/pre[1] and excludes a real /backups/pre1 instead. The consequence follows from shared_snapshots (commands.rs:3349-3352). The main restore fills /backups/pre[1], so the 'exists, not inode 256, empty' check fails and the else branch runs btrfs subvolume create on an existing path. That fails and the step exits, so the load fails. Meanwhile any real /backups/pre1 is silently left out of the restore. Brackets and the other metacharacters are legal in btrfs subvolume names, so this is a wrong result on real input: S1. No rule wins. Rule 1 does not apply: the escaping helper is a few lines of std. Rule 5 only routes the fix: it changes the plan's glob-file content, so it goes to the user as a behaviour fix rather than into a cleanup commit, and the finding already marks changes_output=true. The finding also notes that the same unescaped pattern applies to the pool, reformat and raw globs.

column4: 2 RA4 item 2 (input: JSON) and H6's quoting rule; RA5 S1 'a shell-quoting hole'
column6: The raw-write sh -c script puts the dump's raw_volume.image into echo "the archiver's dump of {image} failed" with no quoting; the same value is shell_quote'd in dump_argv a few characters earlier.
column7: A layout whose dm_devices[].raw_volume.image is /.bko-holt/raw/vg/$(touch /tmp/pwn).img (or contains a double quote) runs the command substitution in the restore stage with --commit, as root. Reach: a hand-edited or crafted layout only. Real dumps build image from VG/LV names, and LVM's name charset [A-Za-z0-9+_.-] cannot hold these characters.
column8: Build the message with shell_quote(&format!("the archiver's dump of {image} failed")) and use echo {quoted} >&2, or pass image as a positional parameter (sh -c '…"$1"…' sh IMAGE). Test: thin_restore with image containing $( and " asserting the script contains them only inside single quotes.
column9: confirmed: At c4917fc, holt/src/load/rawvol.rs around lines 118-126 (thin_restore's write closure) reads image straight from the layout with s(&r, "image"). It passes image to dump_argv, where each word goes through shell_quote. The same image is then put into the sh -c script raw, as echo "the archiver's dump of {image} failed". Inside double quotes the shell still runs $(...) and backticks, and a " in the value ends the quote. A layout whose image holds those characters therefore runs code as root in the restore stage. The script runs on every --commit raw-volume restore, because the [ ... ] || test is part of its text even when the dump succeeds. Nothing in load checks the image value, and the layout is plain JSON a user can edit. Real dumps are safe: qubes::raw_volumes builds image from VG and LV names, which LVM's character set keeps clean. The reviewer states that limit correctly. The doc's S1 definition names 'a shell-quoting hole' with no exception for inputs only a crafted file can reach, so S1 stands. Rule 5 does not drop the finding. The fix changes the printed plan text, so it goes to the user rather than into a cleanup commit, which matches the finding's changes_output=true. The message the shell prints at run time stays the same.

column6: The writing stages' dry run prints each command's shell() unscrubbed, and run_cmd logs the same text to load.log (which the boot stage copies into the restored system). plan::run passes the same text through redact::scrub_recovery_keys.
column7: A layout that carries an Ubuntu Core recovery key, for example a dump from before main.rs:211 scrubbed dumps, or a hand-edited one: `bko-holt load L --through mount` (no --commit) prints the key on stdout, and a committed run writes it into RUN_DIR/log/load.log and the restored /var/log/bko-holt/. plan prints <recovery-key> for the same layout. Not reachable from a dump the current bko-holt writes.
column8: Apply scrub_recovery_keys to out before exec::run returns and to the text inside log_line. Test: exec dry run on a layout with a key-shaped string expecting <recovery-key>.
column9: confirmed: exec::run's dry run (exec.rs:115-118) appends c.shell() for each command with no scrub, and the committed path logs through run_cmd/log_line unscrubbed. plan::run (plan.rs:290) passes its output through redact::scrub_recovery_keys with the contract 'Never a recovery key… whatever the layout held'. The same layout text therefore prints scrubbed in plan and unscrubbed in the stage dry run. main.rs:211 scrubs dumps today, so current dumps can't reach it. That makes it a defence-in-depth gap rather than a live leak: S2, not S1.

column4: 3 RA4 item 3 (errors carry what failed; none lost)
column6: Failures to create RUN_DIR/log or open load.log are discarded (let _ = …; .ok()), but a failing stage still tells the user 'the log is RUN_DIR/log/load.log'.
column7: RUN_DIR isn't writable (a rescue image whose /var/run is read-only). The run goes on with no log. When a command then fails, the message points to a load.log that doesn't exist, and report-bug finds no log to include.
column8: Keep the io::Error, and either refuse --commit without a log or say 'no log (RUN_DIR/log/load.log: {e})' in that message. Test: exec with RUN_DIR unwritable (sysroot test hook) expecting the no-log wording.
column9: confirmed: exec.rs:89-90 discard both errors: `let _ = create_dir_all(...)` and `.open(...).ok()`. log_line on None does nothing, yet on a command failure line 141 still says 'the log is {RUN_DIR}/log/load.log'. The trigger (an unwritable RUN_DIR) is unlikely, but the claim to the user can be false and the io::Error is lost. Error handling, S2. The suggested wording change alters output, so rule 5 sends it to the user.

column4: 2 Book ch. 9 (panics only for bugs, never for bad input); std str slicing docs (panics off a char boundary)
column6: limine() slices each limine.conf line with t[..key.len()], which panics when that byte index falls inside a multi-byte character.
column7: You run `bko-holt load --reformat /=xfs` (or =ext4) on a Limine system (CachyOS, Omarchy) whose limine.conf has the entry line `/Ubuntu 中文版`. That line is 17 bytes and 版 sits at bytes 14..17. The first key, `cmdline:`, slices t[..8], which is fine. The next key, `kernel_cmdline:` (15 bytes), slices t[..15]. That panics with 'byte index 15 is not a char boundary'. `bko-holt rewrite` aborts (exit 101) partway through: /etc/fstab and the cmdline files are already rewritten, limine.conf is not, and the boot stage fails.
column8: Compare without slicing the str: `t.as_bytes().get(..key.len()).is_some_and(|p| p.eq_ignore_ascii_case(key.as_bytes()))`. Keep `cut` as it is, since it is only used after a match, and a match means the first key.len() bytes are ASCII. Test: add a non-ASCII entry title line, e.g. `/Ubuntu 中文版`, to rewrite::tests::command_lines and assert that the kernel_cmdline line below it is still rewritten.
column9: confirmed: At c4917fc, holt/src/load/rewrite.rs:235 tests `t.len() >= key.len() && t[..key.len()].eq_ignore_ascii_case(key)` on every line of limine.conf, and nothing skips comment or title lines first. The file comes from read_to_string in Run::edit, so it is valid UTF-8 and may contain non-ASCII text. `/Ubuntu 中文版` is 17 bytes and 版 sits at bytes 14..17, so `cmdline:` (t[..8]) passes and `kernel_cmdline:` (t[..15]) panics off a char boundary. Any line of 8 or more bytes with a multi-byte character across byte 8 or 15 does the same, including localized titles and comments. Run::rewrite edits /etc/fstab, /etc/kernel/cmdline, /etc/default/grub, /etc/default/limine and /etc/cmdline.d before it reaches the limine.conf files in boot_dirs, so the panic leaves a half-rewritten target, as the finding says. holt has no catch_unwind (git grep finds none). This is a panic on real input, which the S1 definition names, and it goes against the Book ch. 9 rule. None of our rules wins: the byte-slice fix needs no dependency, works on 1.85, and changes no output for input that works today.

column4: 2 RA5 S1 (shell-quoting hole); the crate's own convention of super::shell_quote on every interpolated path (load/zfs_be.rs, load/truenas.rs, load/abroot.rs)
column6: qubes_boot_cmds puts the load target into three `sh -c` scripts without quoting it: the os-prober bind mount (100), its umount (102) and the Xen-entry grep (104).
column7: parse_args accepts any absolute --target other than /, for example `--target "/mnt/bko target"`. On a Qubes restore, line 100 runs `[ ! -e /mnt/bko target/usr/bin/os-prober ] || mount --bind /mnt/bko target/usr/bin/true /mnt/bko target/usr/bin/os-prober`. The test fails with 'unexpected operator' (status 2), mount gets four operands and fails, and the boot stage stops. Line 104 would grep `/mnt/bko` and `target/boot/grub2/grub.cfg` as two separate files.
column8: Quote the paths: `let (qp, qt) = (shell_quote(&p), shell_quote(t));`, then `format!("[ ! -e {qp} ] || mount --bind {qt}/usr/bin/true {qp}")`, `format!("! grep -q ' {p} ' ... || umount {qp}")`, and `shell_quote(&format!("{t}{cfg}"))` in the grep. shell_quote leaves a safe word bare, so the plan text stays byte-identical for /mnt/bko-target and any other safe target. Separately, the mountinfo grep on line 102 can never match a path containing a space, because mountinfo escapes it as \040. Switching to `mountpoint -q {qp} && umount {qp}`, as load/zfs_be.rs:143 does, would fix that, but it changes output and goes to the user. Test: a plan test with --target containing a space that runs the three scripts through sh against a temp tree.
column9: confirmed: Checked at c4917fc. holt/src/load/qubes.rs:100, :102 and :104 build `sh -c` scripts from `{t}` and `{p}` (p = t + "/usr/bin/os-prober") with no quoting. parse_args in load/mod.rs:331-336 only requires --target to be absolute and not "/", so a target containing a space, a quote or a glob character gets through. For `--target "/mnt/bko target"`, the test on :100 gets extra operands and mount gets four. Line :104 makes grep read two separate files. The shell also word-splits `{cfg}` on :104, and cfg comes from the dump's boot.xen.grub_cfg. RA5 lists any shell-quoting hole as S1, so the severity is right. None of our rules wins. The fix doesn't break rule 5, because shell_quote in mod.rs:507 leaves safe words bare and the plan text stays byte-identical for normal targets. It needs no dependency (rule 1) and doesn't touch the forks (rule 3). The mountinfo \040 point and the switch to mountpoint -q belong to the user, as the finding itself says. One thing for the fixer: commands.rs:4058 has the same unquoted os-prober bind, and commands.rs:3511/3513/3618 interpolate `{t}` unquoted in sh -c too. A spaced target would hit those first, but that is more of the same hole, not a refutation.

column4: 2 RA5 S1 (shell-quoting hole); Cmd::shell quotes argv words, so the sh -c wrapper is what drops the quoting
column6: The snapcore-boot-areas step puts the path of the running bko-holt (std::env::current_exe) and the dump's disk name into an `sh -c` string unquoted. Only the layout path gets shell_quote.
column7: Say bko-holt runs from a stick mounted at `/run/media/u/BKO STICK/bko-holt` and restores an Ubuntu Core 24 dump. The boot stage then runs `sh -c '/run/media/u/BKO STICK/bko-holt snapcore-boot-areas ...'`, gets 'sh: /run/media/u/BKO: not found', and fails. The gadget's MBR code and BIOS Boot core.img are not written back.
column8: Minimal fix that keeps the output: `format!("{} snapcore-boot-areas {} {} /dev/{tgt}", shell_quote(&exe), shell_quote(&self.opts.layout), shell_quote(&disk))`. This is byte-identical for safe paths. The cleaner form, `Cmd::new(&[&exe, "snapcore-boot-areas", &self.opts.layout, &disk, &format!("/dev/{tgt}")])` with no sh, changes the plan text, so it goes to the user. Test: a snapcore plan test whose exe path contains a space; this needs current_exe injected, or a check that the generated words go through shell_quote.
column9: confirmed: Confirmed from the code at c4917fc. In holt/src/load/snapcore.rs:240-241, `exe` comes from std::env::current_exe() and goes into `Cmd::new(&["sh","-c", &format!("{exe} snapcore-boot-areas {} {disk} /dev/{tgt}", shell_quote(&self.opts.layout))])`. Only the layout is quoted, so a space or shell metacharacter in the exe path splits the word or is run by the shell. The project's own sibling code shows the intended pattern: rawvol.rs:117-127 builds a similar sh -c script and passes `shell_quote(&exe)`. Every other current_exe use (commands.rs 3986/4782/4849, other/load.rs) passes exe as an argv word with no shell. The command has no .warns(), so a broken path fails the boot stage loudly and the MBR and BIOS Boot core.img are not written back. The rust-audit.md RA5 severity list names "a shell-quoting hole" as S1, and no rule in "Our rules that win" applies: the shell_quote fix keeps the output byte-identical for safe paths because shell_quote returns safe strings unchanged, so rule 5 is not at stake. Limits on reachability: the shipped images install /usr/local/bin/bko-holt, which has no space, so the failure needs bko-holt run from somewhere else (for example a mounted stick path with a space). `disk` and `tgt` are kernel names from the layout and the mapping (vda, sda, nvme0n1), so in practice they are not part of the hole. Quoting them costs nothing, but the real defect is the unquoted exe.

column4: 3 API Guidelines C-GOOD-ERR (errors say what failed); RA4 item 3
column6: When two disks carry the same gadget partlabel, find() refuses that role ('N partitions are named ...'), and read() then also refuses it as 'no partition is named ...'. That second refusal is false and contradicts the first.
column7: Dump an Ubuntu Core system with a second UC disk attached, so that vda and vdb both have ubuntu-seed, ubuntu-boot, ubuntu-save and ubuntu-data. boot.snapcore.refusals, and the message refusal() joins from it, read: '2 partitions are named ubuntu-seed (vda1, vdb1): another Ubuntu Core disk is attached; dump with --only-disk ...; ...; Ubuntu Core: no partition is named ubuntu-seed (the pc gadget's four are ...)'. That happens once per role, so eight refusals, four of them wrong.
column8: Have find() return the roles it found ambiguous (or the roles it handled at all), and in read() skip the 'no partition is named' refusal for those roles. Test: a snapcore::tests case with two disks that each carry the four partlabels; assert exactly one refusal per role and none saying 'no partition is named'. This changes the dump's refusals text, so it goes to the user (rule 5).
column9: confirmed: snapcore.rs at c4917fc: find() (276-299) pushes the 'N partitions are named X' problem and `continue`s without adding the role to `out`. read() (381-388) then pushes 'Ubuntu Core: no partition is named X' for every role that has no entry in `found`. So each ambiguous role gets two contradictory refusals, and refusal() (643) joins both. The dump refuses either way, so no wrong result, but the error text is false: C-GOOD-ERR, S2. Rule 5 doesn't drop it. It sends the message change to the user, which the fix already says.

column4: 6 RA4 item 6 (duplication between modules); Effective Rust / Rust Design Patterns (one abstraction per mechanism)
column6: The private read-only mount sequence (mkdir under /run/bko-holt, mount -o ro..., read, umount, rmdir, warn if still mounted) exists four times: abroot::with_mounted (279), truenas::be_version (76), zfsbootmenu::inactive_boot (293) and boot::read_unmounted_esp (boot.rs:822). It comes with three copies of `safe()` (abroot.rs:271 without '+', truenas.rs:57, zfsbootmenu.rs:286) and three READ_AT constants beside boot::UNMOUNTED_ESP_MOUNTS.
column7: No wrong result today. The copies have already drifted, though. abroot's version checks may_mount and fstype. truenas and zbm check sys.privileged and safe(). boot's version checks neither. abroot's safe() rejects '+' and the other two accept it. A fix to one copy, for example about what to do when umount fails, has to be found and repeated three more times.
column8: Add one `fn with_ro_mount<R>(sys: &Sys, who: &str, ty: &str, opts: &str, dev: &str, at: &str, f: impl FnOnce(&str) -> R) -> Option<R>` in sys.rs or mounts.rs that takes each caller's warning texts or a prefix, so every message stays verbatim. Add one `safe_name(name, extra: &[u8])`. Make abroot's generic with_mounted the template. The scenarios tests that assert those warnings (scenarios.rs 981-1222, 5600-5644, 5963) prove nothing changed.
column9: confirmed: The four copies are there: abroot::with_mounted (279-304), truenas::be_version (76-98), zfsbootmenu::inactive_boot (293-317) and boot::read_unmounted_esp (821-838). Each does the same create_dir_all/mount/f/umount/rmdir/still-mounted warn sequence. There are three READ_AT constants equal to boot::UNMOUNTED_ESP_MOUNTS ('/run/bko-holt'). There are three safe() copies, and abroot's (271) lacks '+' where truenas's and zbm's allow it. One detail is off: abroot also checks sys.privileged and safe(), as well as may_mount and fstype. That doesn't change the finding. Duplicated logic is S2.

column4: 6 RA4 items 5-6; Rust Design Patterns (put shared behaviour on the type)
column6: json::Value has no mutable accessor. reformat.rs carries private obj/get_mut/put/storage_list helpers (510-535). abroot::add_to_boot (483-495), Dump::require_headers (snapcore.rs:625-631), qubes::thin_usage (319-345) and qubes::raw_volumes (263-266) each hand-roll `iter_mut().find(|(k, _)| k == ...)` ladders to reach a key.
column7: No wrong result today. Each module re-derives key lookup on a Vec<(String, Value)>, and the copies differ: put() replaces in place, add_to_boot pushes, qubes retains and then pushes. thin_usage nests three levels of `let (true, Value::Arr(..)) = (k == ..., v) else { continue }` just to reach storage.lvm.volume_groups[].logical_volumes[].
column8: Move reformat's get_mut/put into json.rs as `Value::get_mut(&mut self, key)`, `Value::at_mut(&mut self, path)` and `Value::put(&mut self, key, v)` with Obj::put's replace-in-place semantics, and use them in the five places. At these call sites no key exists before the push (each add_to_boot runs once, report.rs:1663-1667), so key order and output do not change. The corpus round trips prove it.
column9: confirmed: json.rs has get/at but no mutable accessor on Value. Only Obj::put exists, on the builder. reformat.rs 510-535 defines private obj/get_mut/put/storage_list. abroot::add_to_boot (483-498) nests iter_mut loops to reach kernels.installed. Dump::require_headers loops with iter_mut to replace 'refusals'. qubes::thin_usage nests `let (true, Value::Arr(..)) = (k == .., v)` three levels deep. qubes raw_volumes does retain+push. The fix stays inside rule 1, since holt's own reader gains the methods. Duplicated logic is S2.

column4: 6 RA4 item 6 (duplication between modules)
column6: The verbatim-restore boot stage is copied four times: abroot_boot (248), ostree_boot (load/ostree.rs:173), snapcore_boot (load/snapcore.rs:224) and transactional_boot (load/transactional.rs:605). Each repeats the same parts: gate note, atimes 'if-missing', a 'what' string pushed both to notes and as Cmd::note, `sh -c check_script(..).warns()`, efi_entries when uefi && !no_nvram, `mkdir -p` plus `cp -a RUN_DIR/log/.`, then boot_tail. Their check scripts also repeat the `err() { errs=...; nbad=... }` accumulator and its error tail, and the `of(layout)` lookups of boot.X appear four times, plus Builder::truenas and Builder::zbm.
column7: No wrong result today. Every new image-based distro copies about 20 lines of frame and a shell prelude, and an ordering change in one frame (log before or after efi_entries, say) has to be made four times. Golden plans pin each copy separately.
column8: Add a Builder helper that takes (gate text, what, checks, extra cmds, log dir) and emits the frame in today's order. Add `fn sh_err_prelude(prefix: &str) -> String`, which yields today's exact err() text, so ostree's per-entry counting variant stays its own. Add one `boot_section(layout, key)`. golden_plans.rs and the corpus prove the output is unchanged.
column9: downgraded: The frames are less alike than claimed. snapcore_boot makes no efi_entries call, uses self.atimes instead of atimes_cmd, and puts boot_areas and grub-editenv between the check and the log. ostree_boot writes its log only when ostree_var resolves and adds a SELinux LABEL_PY step. transactional_boot has key files before atimes, never pushes its 'what' to self.notes, and has a large middle: btrfs mount, BLS/hc scripts, mount-point labels, umount, grub2-bios-setup. What they really share is about five lines: the gate note, the atimes line, the what note and mkdir+cp of the log. A frame helper would need several injection hooks to keep today's order, which makes it a worse abstraction than the copies. The repeated err() prelude and the four of() functions are real but small. That is polish, not duplicated logic a maintainer needs fixed.

column4: 6 RA4 item 6; Effective Rust (reuse types over re-deriving)
column6: KEY=VALUE files with last-key-wins lookup are parsed in five places, each with its own rev().find(): abroot::Config::get (abroot.rs:63), ostree::parse_ini + ini_get (ostree.rs:37/56), transactional::parse_state plus two ad-hoc rev-find closures (transactional.rs:45/115/126), snapcore::Env (84-105) and qubes::default_grub_var (qubes.rs:388). boot::parse_shell_assignments and osrel::parse also exist.
column7: No wrong result today. The formats really do differ (GKeyFile sections, shell quoting, raw modeenv values), but the lookup layer is copied, and a reader has to check each copy to know whether the first or the last duplicate wins.
column8: Keep each format's parser. Have them return one shared key/value type, snapcore::Env moved to e.g. crate::kv with get/some/list, so the last-wins lookup is written once. The parsers stay as they are, so output does not change.
column9: refuted: The 'copied lookup layer' is a one-line `iter().rev().find()` over different shapes that one type can't share. abroot::Config::get is a case-insensitive lookup over JSON Values (viper semantics) of abroot.json, not a KEY=VALUE file. ostree::ini_get matches (section, key) triples. qubes::default_grub_var is a streaming last-assignment scan with its own quote stripping. transactional uses parse_state's Vec plus rev().find, and snapcore::Env is already the type. A shared kv type would fit only transactional and snapcore. The claimed failure, that a reader can't tell which duplicate wins, doesn't hold either: each one's doc comment says the last wins (Config::get, Env, default_grub_var). Too little shared logic to be an S2 finding.

column4: 2 std::fs docs (read_to_string and write follow symlinks); RA4 item 2 (file names as input)
column6: Run::edit reads and writes each restored file with std::fs::read_to_string and std::fs::write, which follow symlinks. An absolute link in the restored tree therefore resolves against the rescue system's root, not TARGET. Meanwhile is_file/is_dir use symlink_metadata, so the same file is treated two ways.
column7: You restore with --reformat /=ext4 into /mnt/bko-target, and the restored tree has /etc/kernel/cmdline as an absolute symlink (for example to /etc/kernel/cmdline.d/base, or any absolute target). rewrite edits whatever that path is on the rescue system, if it exists, and leaves the restored file unchanged. Then `--check` fails later on rootflags=subvol=. In the other direction, a restored /etc/fstab that is a symlink is reported as 'not there' (line 350). No distribution is known to ship links at these paths: the case is constructed, but the code behaviour is verified.
column8: In edit(), check symlink_metadata first. For a symlink, either resolve it inside the target, as ostree::resolve does (relative to the tree's top, depth-limited), or skip it with a logged `warning:` line. Then make the fstab existence check use the same resolution. Output is unchanged for regular files; only the symlink case gains a log line. Test: a_target_tree with /etc/kernel/cmdline as an absolute symlink.
column9: confirmed: load/rewrite.rs at c4917fc: Run::edit (336-346) uses std::fs::read_to_string and std::fs::write on PathBufs built as '{target}{p}'. Both follow symlinks, so an absolute link in the restored tree resolves against the rescue system's root. If the rescue has a file there that f changes, the write goes outside the target. Otherwise the read fails and the edit is silently skipped. is_file/is_dir (293-298) use symlink_metadata, so a symlinked /etc/fstab is reported 'not there' (351). commands.rs:3987 shows rewrite runs from the rescue system with the target path, not in a chroot, so the behaviour is real. column4: 2 checklist 2; NetBSD sys/dev/dkwedge/dk.c (trunk): dkwedge_add returns EEXIST for a wedge name already used on any parent disk; dkwedge_gpt.c retries with the GUID string
column6: NetBSD GPT partitions are named NAME=<GPT name> (part_node, and mod.rs:184-197 node_path), but wedge names are unique across the whole system, so a same-named wedge on another attached disk makes newfs and mount act on that other disk.
column7: Restore a NetBSD GPT disk onto wd1 while the source wd0 is still attached and unmounted (booted from the stick). write-table copies the names and GUIDs exactly (load.rs:339), so on wd1 dkwedge_add hits EEXIST for the name, the retry with the GUID string hits EEXIST too, and wd1 gets no wedge ("manual intervention required"). `newfs NAME=root` then resolves to wd0's dk wedge and overwrites the source's root filesystem. node_path also returns the first disk's dkN in hw.disknames order, so readback and status check the wrong disk.
column8: In scan/plan, refuse when a disk that isn't a target has a wedge whose name (or GUID) equals one of the target's GPT entries; dkctl listwedges per disk is already available in labelled.rs. Better, name the target's partitions by (target disk, start LBA), resolved to /dev/dkN at run time the way softraid's find_volume resolves $v. Test: scan plus plan with two disks carrying the same wedge names must refuse.
column9: confirmed: Confirmed from the code at c4917fc and NetBSD trunk. part_node (other/load.rs:29-30) names a NetBSD GPT partition NAME=<GPT label>, and other_newfs (load.rs ~398) keeps NAME= nodes as they are, because only /dev/ nodes get the r prefix. newfs and mount therefore resolve the name system-wide. node_path (other/mod.rs ~184-197) returns the first dkN with that name, taking disks in hw.disknames order. In NetBSD's dk.c, dkwedge_add checks the name against the global dkwedges array, which covers every parent, and returns EEXIST on a match. other_partition writes the source's names and GUIDs exactly (write-table) and then runs dkctl makewedges on the target. Nothing in scan or map_disks looks at wedge names on disks that aren't targets: the duplicate-identity check in target.rs map_disks covers only LVM VG names and UUIDs, and in_use/hard_use cover only the targets. So with --map wd0=wd1 and the source wd0 attached and unmounted, wd0's dk wedge keeps the name root, and `newfs NAME=root` formats wd0's partition. Readback and status also read wd0 through node_path. One detail of the failure case is wrong. dkwedge_gpt.c retries with the GUID string, and that retry succeeds, because wd0's wedge is named root, not the GUID. wd1 gets GUID-named wedges (logged as 'already existed, using <guid>'), not 'no wedge / manual intervention required'. The outcome is the same: the source disk is overwritten. Rule 5 doesn't win: this is a data-loss bug, not a style fix. The fix adds a refusal, so under RA7 it goes to the user first.

column8: For a GPT entry with no label, use NAME=<the entry's unique GUID>, taken from the layout part's uuid. Test: part_node on a GPT Disk whose part has label None and uuid U gives NAME=U.
column9: confirmed: I confirmed this from the code at c4917fc. In layout.rs:136, an empty partlabel becomes label=None. Then the NetBSD arm of part_node (other/load.rs:29-31) matches only (Gpt, Some(l)) to NAME={l}. A GPT partition with no label falls through to /dev/{t}mbr{n}. That is a holt-internal dump name (labelled.rs:212 uses it for MBR partitions only), not a NetBSD device node. For a GPT disk with no disklabel, the partition stage runs `dkctl makewedges` (other/load.rs:373-374), so the partition is only reachable as dkN or NAME=<wedge name>. Names::dev (commands.rs:223) hands the bogus /dev/wd1mbr2 to the format stage. other_newfs turns it into /dev/rwd1mbr2, so newfs fails after the table and wedges are already written, and load stops partway. NetBSD's dkwedge_gpt names a wedge with an empty GPT name by its unique partition GUID, so the proposed fix (NAME=<part uuid>) is right. The dump also records the live wedge name as wedge_name (labelled.rs:280-281), which the fix could use instead. Partitions made with `gpt add` and no -l are real input. A restore that fails halfway on them is a wrong result on real input, so S1 stands. None of our rules applies.
