At other/load.rs:497 the .snap command is built as a format! string that puts {top} into `sh -c` with no quoting, and {top} is opts.target followed by fstab's `file`. That `file` comes from mounts::parse_fstab, which runs unescape and turns \040 back into a space. So a UFS mount at "/srv/web data" splits into several words: `[` errors and the || branch runs touch/rmdir on the wrong paths, or the command just fails. On FreeBSD the probe parses `mount -p` the same way, so it is likely to mark snap_dir false for such a mount, and the line does run. Case 2 holds as well. part_node (load.rs:29-31) returns `NAME={label}` for a NetBSD GPT partition with a label, and labelled_boot pastes it unquoted into `mount -t msdos {node} {mnt}`. A GPT label can contain spaces, so the mount fails and the ESP gets no BOOTX64.EFI. Case 3 holds too: load/mod.rs:331-336 only checks that --target is absolute and not /. The same unquoted target also turns up in the Linux paths of load/commands.rs (for example 3511 and 4058), so the problem goes wider than other/. The duid/geli/{src} sites are weaker, since they need a hand-edited layout or a device name with odd characters, but they are the same kind of hole. The fix holds up. shell_quote (load/mod.rs:507) returns safe words unchanged, so the corpus plans stay byte-identical. It is a correctness fix, not a style change, so rule 5 does not win, and no other rule applies. A shell-quoting hole is S1 by the RA5 definition.

column4: 2 checklist 2; parttable::read_table semantics (reads the GPT at LBA 1 of the sector size it's given)
column6: illumos (and Haiku, haiku.rs:59) hard-code a 512-byte sector for every disk, so on a 4Kn disk read_table misses the GPT at byte 4096 and reports the protective MBR as an MBR table with one 0xee partition.
column7: OmniOS on an NVMe namespace formatted with 4096-byte LBAs: read_mbr finds the 0xee entry, read_gpt(src, 512) finds nothing at byte 512 or in the last 512 bytes, and read_table returns Table::Mbr. The dump then lists no slices, no rpool member and no ESP, and load writes a one-entry MBR.
column8: Get the logical block size from the system (illumos: prtvtoc or iostat -En; Haiku: none without ioctls, so try it), or call read_table again with 4096 when 512 finds only a protective MBR. Test: read_disk on a 4096-sector GPT MemSource with RawDisk.sector 512.
column9: confirmed: Confirmed from the code at c4917fc. illumos.rs:48 and haiku.rs:59 build every RawDisk with sector: 512, while freebsd.rs:30 reads the real sectorsize. read_disk (mod.rs:234) passes d.sector straight to parttable::read_table. With ss=512, read_gpt (parttable.rs:240-247) looks for the primary header at byte 512 and the backup in the last 512 bytes. On a 4Kn disk the primary header is at byte 4096 and the backup starts at size-4096, so it finds neither. read_table (316-328) then falls through to Table::Mbr with the single 0xee entry, which is not empty. The dump comes out wrong: no slices, no rpool member, no ESP, and logical_sector_size 512. If illumos physio refuses unaligned 512-byte reads on a 4Kn raw node, the result is still wrong (no table at all). 4Kn NVMe namespaces are real hardware that illumos blkdev supports, so this is a wrong result on real input, which is S1 by RA5's definition. No rule of ours wins. Rule 5 only means the fix (a different logical_sector_size and table in the output) goes to the user as a behaviour change. It doesn't make the defect a style matter. Haiku on 4Kn is rarer, but its code path has the same flaw.

column4: 2 checklist 2 (integer arithmetic on input checked); Cargo.toml profile.release has no overflow-checks
column6: read_disk multiplies the partition table's LBAs by the sector size unchecked (`start * d.sector`, `sectors * d.sector`), and parttable keeps GPT entries that lie outside the disk (it only records a problem).
column7: A CRC-valid GPT (crafted, or written by a buggy tool) with an entry whose first_lba is 2^56 on a FreeBSD, NetBSD, illumos or Haiku disk: a debug or test build panics with 'attempt to multiply with overflow'. Release wraps instead, so OffsetSource starts at a wrapped offset, probe_all reports another region's filesystem as this partition's, and the size wraps too, which breaks esp_image's 4 GiB bound.
column8: Use checked_mul and skip the entry with sys.warn (or a partition problem). Test: read_disk on a MemSource GPT whose entry has first_lba = u64::MAX / 512 + 1.
column9: downgraded: The arithmetic is real and unchecked. At c4917fc, read_gpt (parttable.rs:281-293) keeps any non-zero entry and only adds a problem string when it lies outside the usable area. Nothing bounds first_lba/last_lba against the disk, and Cargo.toml's [profile.release] has no overflow-checks. The finding misplaces the first overflow, though. read_disk calls table.partition_json(n, d.sector) before line 238, and gpt_part_json (parttable.rs:427-428) already computes `p.first_lba * ss` and `sectors * ss` unchecked. That is where a debug or test build panics; mod.rs:238-239 is only the second spot. The MBR path cannot overflow, because u32 LBAs times the sector size fit in u64. In release, 2^56*512 wraps to 0, so the probe reads from the disk start and reports that region's filesystem. I'm downgrading from S1 because S1 means a panic or wrong result on real input, and this needs an LBA of at least 2^55 (2^52 at 4K sectors) in a GPT whose CRCs are valid. Random damage fails the CRC check. A realistic broken disk, such as a bigger disk's image dd'd onto a smaller one, has LBAs past the end but far below the overflow range, so it reads short instead of wrapping. Only a deliberately crafted table on the machine being backed up reaches it, and no test or corpus input does. It belongs under S2's input-checking and error-handling class. The fix must also cover gpt_part_json's start_bytes and size_bytes. Skipping such an entry, as proposed, changes the layout JSON for that case. Under rule 5 that is a behaviour change for the user to decide; a style cleanup can't carry it. Keeping the entry and saturating or omitting the byte fields is the alternative.

column7: bko-holt run where BLOCKSIZE isn't K (a non-login ssh shell, or a script): the header says "512-blocks" and storage.swaps[].size_bytes is twice the real size. column8: Share one header-aware parse between freebsd.rs, labelled.rs and dfly.rs, or run `swapctl -lk`.
column9: confirmed: Confirmed. freebsd.rs:296-298 multiplies the column by 1024 and never reads the header. dfly.rs:190 and labelled.rs:352 parse the "N-blocks" header (default 512). column4: 3 Checklist 3 (the caller never parses an error string to decide what to do), D4 (a typed error wherever a caller matches on an error's text), API Guidelines C-GOOD-ERR
column6: corpus_build decides whether a raw dump's check_plan failure stops the dump (a leak) or is reported but still built (a plan diff, a map-back failure). It decides this by matching the prefix of bugreport::check_plan's String error (failure_class, 284-291). The privacy gate of the corpus therefore rests on the wording of messages in another module.
column7: Say bugreport.rs rewords "left in the redacted dump's plan" (bugreport.rs:575) or "the plan of the redacted dump differs" (571). failure_class then returns "another failure", which is a hard stop. This is fail-safe for leaks, so nothing leaks today. But a reworded map-back message silently turns a soft failure into a hard one. And a new check_plan error that begins with one of the soft prefixes but means a leak would be built into the corpus.
column8: Give check_plan a hand-written error enum (Leak, MapBack, PlanDiffers, NotJson, Args) whose Display keeps today's texts, then match on the variant in build_one and failure_class. No new dependency (rule 1). The message texts stay byte for byte, so plans and report text do not change.
column9: confirmed: corpus_build.rs failure_class (284-291) matches prefixes of check_plan's String error. build_one uses the class to choose a hard stop (class starts with 'left in', 'not JSON' or 'another failure') or a soft FAIL. The prefixes match bugreport.rs:571 ('the plan of the redacted dump differs') and 575 ('left in the redacted dump's plan'). This is exactly the case D4 names for a typed error: a caller matching on an error's text. It is fail-safe today: an unknown text becomes 'another failure', a hard stop. build_one also reruns its own leak checks on the redacted dump and its plan, so the privacy risk is smaller than the summary suggests. Still a real error-handling and API-shape item. A hand-written enum is allowed under rule 1, and rule 5 holds if Display keeps the texts.

column4: 1 Rustonomicon/std: FFI constants proved against the platform headers
column6: FICLONE is hard-coded as 0x4004_9409, which is the asm-generic `_IOW(0x94, 9, int)`. linux.rs builds its ioctl numbers with `libc::_IOW::<T>()`, which encodes them per architecture, but this one does not.
column7: cfg(target_os = "linux") also admits powerpc64, mips and sparc. There `_IOC_WRITE` is 4 with dirshift 29, so FICLONE is 0x8004_9409. On those targets `restore --clone-from` would send an unknown ioctl, get ENOTTY on every file, and never clone (it falls back, so no data goes wrong). No target BackOtter ships (x86_64, aarch64) is affected. The arch encoding is unverified in this session: it comes from Linux's arch/powerpc/include/uapi/asm/ioctl.h, and I did not read that header here. The inconsistency with linux.rs is verified.
column8: `const FICLONE: libc::Ioctl = libc::_IOW::<libc::c_int>(0x94, 9);` as linux.rs does for FS_IOC_FSSETXATTR. Optionally add a unit test asserting it equals 0x4004_9409 on x86_64/aarch64.
column9: confirmed: Line 309 is `const FICLONE: libc::Ioctl = 0x4004_9409;`, while linux.rs builds every ioctl number with `libc::_IOW`/`_IOR` and tests the values. On powerpc, mips and sparc Linux, `_IOC_WRITE` is 4 at shift 29, giving 0x8004_9409, so the hard-coded value is wrong on targets the cfg admits. The harm is limited. clone_contents returns the errno, clone_over_with removes the temp file and returns CloneFailed::Failed, and the restore falls back. No shipped target is affected. The bar's FFI item (constants proved against the headers) still makes this a real defect, and there is no rule conflict.

column4: 3 API Guidelines C-GOOD-ERR; std Error::source (no lost source)
column6: `path_error` rebuilds the error as `io::Error::new(kind, format!("{op} {path}: {err}"))`. That drops the original error, its `raw_os_error()` and any source, at about 72 call sites across osattrs.
column7: An error passed through path_error has `raw_os_error() == None`, so `unsupported()` (1824) and `xattr_unsupported()` (1002) can no longer classify it. `acl_set_error(err, source)` (1713) exists only to work around that: the callers (freebsd_netbsd.rs:169, illumos.rs:180) must pass the errno twice, once wrapped and once raw. Any new caller that classifies after wrapping gets the wrong answer: a file system without ACLs would be counted as an error for --strict-exit.
column8: A small `PathError { op: &'static str, path: PathBuf, source: io::Error }` with the same Display text (`{op} {path}: {source}`) and `source()`, wrapped as `io::Error::new(source.kind(), PathError{..})`. Classifiers then look through it (`get_ref()` + downcast) as restore_error_counts already does for `Unsupported`. acl_set_error can then take one argument. Messages stay byte-identical.
column9: confirmed: path_error (line 1703) is `io::Error::new(err.kind(), format!(...))`, which keeps the kind but drops raw_os_error and the source, at 72 call sites. acl_set_error(err, source) takes the raw error a second time only to recover the errno. Its two callers, freebsd_netbsd.rs:169 and illumos.rs:180, show the workaround. The checklist's item 3 ("no lost source") names this directly. No live misclassification turned up. Every errno classifier (`unsupported`, `xattr_unsupported`) runs before wrapping, and restore_error_counts goes by kind, which survives. So the failure is latent, not current. column4: 1 RA4 item 1 (FFI semantics of FS_IOC_FSSETXATTR per file system) and item 6 (logic diverged from its twin put_back_restricting_with); RA5 S1 wrong result
column6: restore_flags_with's btrfs-compression path sets i/a through FS_IOC_FSSETXATTR and never checks the result. put_back_restricting_with (858-867) does check, because on OpenZFS 2.2 that ioctl reads fsx_xflags as FS_*_FL flags, and there FS_XFLAG_APPEND (0x10) is FS_IMMUTABLE_FL.
column7: A btrfs source file has the btrfs.compression property and chattr +a. It is restored onto Ubuntu 24.04's OpenZFS 2.2. The compression path is taken whatever the target is (restore_file_flags 685-688 looks only at the node's xattrs). set_compression fails, and set_late still runs add_xflags(FS_XFLAG_APPEND). Under the OpenZFS 2.2 behaviour that linux.rs 796-801 documents and the 'zfs a' tests model, ZFS sets immutable, not append-only, and the call returns Ok. The file comes back immutable, so later writes and renames by the restore or the user fail. Verdict PLAUSIBLE: the OpenZFS 2.2 behaviour comes from the code's own comments and tests (ubuntu24, round 15), not from OpenZFS source checked here.
column8: Take the compression path only when the file is on btrfs (is_on(&f, BTRFS_SUPER_MAGIC)). Or, after add_xflags, check get_flags() == own|first|late and fall back to set(own|first|late) when it differs, as put_back_restricting_with does. Test: extend restore_flags_calls with a ZFS-2.2 mock add_xflags (f |= xflags, as put_back_restricting_with_zfs_xflags does) and assert the final flags are FS_APPEND_FL, not FS_IMMUTABLE_FL. No message or exit code changes; only the restored flags in the failure case.
column9: confirmed: The finding holds against rustic_core 3fd3921 linux.rs (line 964 matches; 695d676 has the same code). restore_file_flags (osattrs.rs 615, linux.rs ~666-700) takes the compression value from the node's xattrs, not from the target file system. So any node carrying btrfs.compression goes down restore_flags_with's compression branch on any target, ZFS included. On ZFS, set_compression fails, because the VFS has no handler for a 'btrfs.' xattr prefix. set_late still runs, and its add_xflags closure does get_fsxattr, then xflags |= FS_XFLAG_APPEND (0x10), then set_fsxattr. It only maps the error and never reads the flags back. The twin put_back_restricting_with (839-867) does read them back: it calls get() == want after add_xflags and falls back to set(want). Its doc comment and test put_back_restricting_with_zfs_xflags ('zfs a') say why: OpenZFS 2.2 reads fsx_xflags as FS_*_FL, and 0x10 there is FS_IMMUTABLE_FL. clear_restricting_with (796-801) records the same behaviour as seen on ubuntu24 in round 15. From what I recall of OpenZFS 2.2's zpl_ioctl_setxattr, it passes fsx_xflags straight to __zpl_ioctl_setflags, which fits; I did not check that against the OpenZFS source. Under that behaviour the call returns Ok and the file is immutable, not append-only: a wrong result that nothing reports. A related case is worse: with i+a, the 0x8 bit reads as FS_SYNC_FL, which ZFS 2.2 refuses (EOPNOTSUPP), so both flags are dropped with an Unsupported warning, which the suggested readback-and-set fallback would also fix. The input is rare but real: a btrfs file with the compression property and chattr +a, restored by rustic-bko onto an Ubuntu 24.04 host on ZFS 2.2, a guest we test. None of our rules wins. The fix stays inside our own BackOtter function (rule 3 is not involved) and changes no message or exit code (rule 5 is not involved).

column4: 1 RA4 item 1 (no wrong behaviour on any target the cfgs admit; FFI types vs headers); sparse.rs:140-141 states the same hazard and handles it
column6: is_on (270) and is_bcachefs_path (1092) read statfs.f_type with u32::try_from. On 32-bit glibc f_type is a signed 32-bit word, so BCACHEFS_SUPER_MAGIC 0xca451a4e comes out negative and is never matched. Plain fstatfs/statfs on 32-bit glibc also fail with EOVERFLOW on file systems whose block counts pass 32 bits.
column7: Build for i686-unknown-linux-gnu or armv7-unknown-linux-gnueabihf (linux.rs is cfg(target_os = "linux"), so these targets are admitted) and back up a bcachefs file whose project ID changed since its inode was read in. file_projid skips the bcachefs_effective.project xattr and records the stale or 0 ID. On restore, prepare_dir_for_options and the 0-project-ID reset are skipped, so entries do not inherit their directory's bcachefs options. On a >16 TiB file system with 4 KiB blocks, fstatfs returns EOVERFLOW, and fill_dos_flags turns that into a per-file 'fstatfs' error. BackOtter's shipped builds are musl (f_type is c_ulong there) and build-backotter.sh refuses *-linux-gnu, so no shipped binary is affected. The libc 0.2.189 field types are unverified here: they come from sparse.rs's own comment and glibc's bits/statfs.h (__fsword_t is int on 32-bit), with no local copy of either.
column8: Use one helper, sparse::fs_type (already 'st.f_type as u32', the low 32 bits), from linux.rs. Make it call fstatfs64/statfs64 on gnu and musl, as lseek already uses lseek64 for the same 32-bit reason. Test: a pure fn taking the raw f_type, asserting that (0xca45_1a4e_u32 as i32) maps to BCACHEFS_SUPER_MAGIC.
column9: confirmed: Confirmed from the code. is_on (linux.rs 262-271) and is_bcachefs_path (1081-1093) both end with u32::try_from(st.f_type), while sparse.rs fs_type (129-149) uses 'st.f_type as u32' and its comment says why: f_type is a signed 32-bit word on 32-bit glibc. So on i686/armv7 gnu, BCACHEFS_SUPER_MAGIC 0xca451a4e (bit 31 set) never matches. file_projid then skips the bcachefs_effective.project xattr, and restore_attributes' project-ID-0 reset (1048) and prepare_dir_for_options (1112) are skipped. ZFS (0x2fc12fc1), XFS and MSDOS magics are positive and unaffected. Plain fstatfs/statfs on non-LFS 32-bit glibc returning EOVERFLOW is a real glibc behaviour, and fill_dos_flags (639) and restore_fat_attrs (492) do turn it into a path_error('fstatfs'). I could not verify the libc 0.2.189 field types locally (there is no registry copy); they rest on sparse.rs's own comment. S2 stands rather than S1: /Users/mchobbit/git/rustic/build-backotter.sh refuses *-linux-gnu targets (lines 40, 51) and maps them to musl, where f_type is c_ulong, so no shipped or tested binary hits it. It is still wrong behaviour on targets the cfgs admit (RA4 item 1). No rule wins: this is our own file (added in fork commit fcac5fa), and the fix changes no output on any shipped target.

column4: 6 RA4 item 6 (duplication between modules); Effective Rust; RA5 S2 duplicated logic
column6: Linux FFI helpers are duplicated across linux.rs and sparse.rs, and the copies have already drifted apart (the finding above).
column7: The duplicates: fstatfs-to-f_type appears three times (linux.rs is_on 262-271 and is_bcachefs_path 1081-1093, sparse.rs fs_type 129-149), and only sparse.rs's copy is right on 32-bit. ZFS_SUPER_MAGIC and BCACHEFS_SUPER_MAGIC are each defined twice (linux.rs 97/100, sparse.rs 153/171). FS_NOCOW_FL is written as a bare literal three times (linux.rs 48 and 60, sparse.rs 175). sparse.rs is_nocow (205-212) repeats linux.rs get_flags (225-232). linux.rs has two xattr growth loops, get_xattr (296-314, fgetxattr) and read_whole (1176-1197). sparse.rs decide (55-57) repeats the errno list of osattrs.rs unsupported().
column8: Keep one pub(super) fs_type and the magic and flag constants in sparse.rs (cfg linux/android), with linux.rs using them. Have is_nocow call a shared get_flags. Write get_xattr as read_whole(|v, n| fgetxattr(fd, name, v, n)). Have decide call super::unsupported. No behaviour change, except that get_xattr then reads values of any size.
column9: confirmed: Every duplicate named was found. fstatfs-to-f_type appears three times (linux.rs is_on and is_bcachefs_path, sparse.rs fs_type), and the copies have drifted on the 32-bit cast (finding 1). ZFS_SUPER_MAGIC and BCACHEFS_SUPER_MAGIC are defined in both files (linux.rs 97/100, sparse.rs 153/171). FS_NOCOW_FL is a bare literal at linux.rs 48 and 60 and a const at sparse.rs 175. sparse.rs is_nocow (205-212) repeats the FS_IOC_GETFLAGS ioctl of linux.rs get_flags (225-232). get_xattr (296-314) is a second growth loop beside read_whole (1176-1197), capped at 64 KiB where read_whole has no cap. The errno list in sparse.rs decide (55-57) is identical to osattrs.rs unsupported() (1824-1829). All three files are ours (fork commits fcac5fa and 7821230), so rule 3 does not apply. RA5 lists duplicated logic as S2. One limit on the fix: sharing across the two files needs pub(super) items under a cfg covering both linux and android, since sparse.rs's copies are cfg linux/android and linux.rs is linux only. The fix sketch already allows for that.

column4: 6 RA4 item 6 (structure, duplication); Rust Design Patterns (module layout)
column6: The same five-OS cfg list, any(target_os = "linux", "android", "freebsd", "illumos", target_vendor = "apple"), appears 18 times in sparse.rs's 768 non-test lines, some with 'test' added and some negated, on each item of the SEEK_HOLE reader.
column7: Adding or removing one OS from the SEEK_HOLE set (DragonFly's comment at 89-92 already discusses it) means editing up to 18 attributes the same way. A missed one either fails to compile or quietly falls back to the blocks-decide path: has_holes (80-100) and backup_reader (354-376) each pair a positive and a negated copy, and those must agree.
column8: Move Extents, HoleReader, lseek, seek_hole, open and holes_now into a submodule (sparse/seek.rs) behind one #[cfg(any(test, ...))], or define the list once with a cfg_aliases-style build.rs alias. The fix is in our own file, so rule 3 is not touched. No behaviour change.
column9: confirmed: The repetition is real, but the count is slightly high. In sparse.rs's 769 non-test lines, the exact five-OS list (linux, android, freebsd, illumos, apple) appears in 16 cfg attributes: 7 bare, 7 with 'test' added, 2 negated. Two more attributes use different OS lists (338 adds solaris, and one negated list has dragonfly and openbsd), so '18' only holds if those variants are counted. The hazard checks out. In has_holes (80-100) and backup_reader (354-376), a positive and a negated copy must agree. In has_holes, an OS added to the positive list but not removed from the negated one would compile: the second 'let first_hole = None' shadows the first and quietly falls back to the blocks deciding. The DragonFly comment (89-92) shows the set is still being discussed. The file is ours, and the submodule fix touches no upstream line. One caveat: the cfg_aliases build.rs option would add a build.rs to upstream's crate, which rule 3 discourages, so the sparse/seek.rs submodule is the variant to take.

column4: 6 RA4 item 6 (files past ~1,500 lines are split candidates along existing seams)
column6: linux.rs is 2,160 lines: about 1,230 of code covering seven separate concerns, plus a 930-line test module. The concerns are inode flags, restricting-flag clear and put-back, ZFS DOS flags, FAT attributes, XFS options, bcachefs project and options, and whole-value xattr reads.
column7: Not a runtime failure. The FAT, ZFS, XFS and bcachefs blocks share only open_for_flags, is_on and the fsxattr ioctls, and they are interleaved: XFS sits at 432-633, ZFS at 635-724, ZFS again at 870-897, bcachefs at 1036-1141.
column8: Split along those seams into linux/{flags,zfs_dos,fat,xfs,bcachefs,xattr}.rs, with the shared ioctl wrappers in linux.rs. Move tests to linux/tests.rs or per submodule. The files are ours, so rule 3 is not involved. No behaviour change.
column9: downgraded: The facts check out: 2,160 lines, tests from 1231, and the interleaving as described (FAT 400-428 and 466-526 even sits between the XFS pieces at 436-462 and 528-633; ZFS at 638-724 and 873-897; bcachefs at 1036-1141). But RA4 item 6 makes a file 'past ~1,500 lines a split candidate', not a defect. The non-test code is about 1,230 lines, under that mark, and the rest is the #[cfg(test)] module. The failure case admits there is no runtime or maintenance failure beyond layout. The concerns share is_on, open_for_flags and the fsxattr/flags ioctls, so a six-file split mostly adds pub(super) plumbing. column6: The checks of the ioctl numbers in fsxattr_ioctls, zfs_dos_ioctls and fat_ioctls run only on target_env = "gnu". BackOtter ships only musl builds (build-backotter.sh refuses -linux-gnu), so those numbers are never checked on a shipped target.
column7: On musl, libc::Ioctl is c_int, so a literal like 0x801c_581f does not fit, which is presumably why the checks are gated to gnu. A wrong _IOR size or type on musl would go unnoticed. Risk is low, because the same libc::_IOR builds both.
column8: Compare `FS_IOC_FSGETXATTR as u32` (and the other ioctls the same way) against the u32 literals, without the target_env gate. Keep the arch gate for _IOC encodings that differ (powerpc, mips, sparc).

column4: 1 RA4 item 1; Rustonomicon (state the invariant a SAFETY comment relies on)
column6: read_whole is a safe fn whose closures do the unsafe lgetxattr and llistxattr calls. The SAFETY comments at 1205 and 1220 depend on read_whole only ever passing (null, 0) or (a live buffer, its length), but read_whole's doc does not promise that.
column7: There is no UB today; both calls in read_whole meet that invariant. A later edit to read_whole, such as reusing a buffer with a stale length, would break the callers' SAFETY claims, and nothing in read_whole's doc would warn the editor.
column8: Add to read_whole's doc: 'call is given either a null pointer and 0, or a pointer to a writable buffer of exactly that many bytes'. Point the two SAFETY comments at it. No behaviour change.

column6: open_for_flags gives the error '<path> was replaced while it was read' for every mismatch. That includes the restore-side callers, which pass listed = None, so the only possible failure there is a type mismatch, and nothing was being read.
column7: A restore-side caller (restore_file_flags, restore_fat_attrs, restore_xfs_options or restore_zfs_dos_flags) is given a path that is now a directory where the node is a file. It reports '... was replaced while it was read', which misleads about the cause.
column8: Use separate messages: 'is not a regular file/directory' when the type differs, and 'was replaced since it was listed' when dev/ino differ. This changes message text, so under rule 5 it goes to the user.

column4: 2 checklist 2 (input: names from the file system); Book ch. 9 / std OsStr docs (names are bytes, not UTF-8); rule 4 parity with restic-bko
column6: list_extattrs turns each extattr name into a String with from_utf8_lossy before it is used to read the value, so the read uses a name that does not exist and the value is lost.
column7: FreeBSD or NetBSD, `setextattr user $'\xff' v f` (or the system namespace as root). Backup: xattr_list (osattrs.rs:1457) gives `user.\u{FFFD}`. xattr::get with that name gets ENOATTR, which becomes Ok(None), so the node keeps `\u{FFFD}` with no value (mapper.rs xattrs_with). For a system extattr, get_system_extattr's ENOATTR is taken as 'removed since the listing' (line 312) and the attribute is dropped without a word. Stock rustic reads the value by its exact OsString name, and restic-bko reads it by its exact Go string name, so this is a regression and a parity break. Two names that convert to the same lossy string also collide.
column8: Return the names as bytes (Vec<Vec<u8>> or OsString via OsStrExt::from_bytes) from list_extattrs. Read each value by its exact bytes, and make the name lossy only when it is stored in the node (as restic-bko's JSON does). In osattrs.rs build `user.` + bytes as an OsString. Test: a portable unit test of the extracted list parser on a 0xff name, plus a FreeBSD/NetBSD guest round trip with setextattr on a non-UTF-8 name.
column9: confirmed: I confirmed the finding from the code on rustic_core backotter (695d676). In freebsd_netbsd.rs, list_extattrs calls String::from_utf8_lossy on each name before using it. The user namespace path then fails: osattrs::xattr_list builds format!("user.{name}"), and xattr_get passes that name to xattr::get, which on BSD strips the `user.` prefix and asks for the replacement-character bytes EF BF BD. That name does not exist, so the call fails with ENOATTR, which the crate returns as Ok(None). mapper.rs xattrs_with then pushes the attribute with value None, so the value is lost without a warning. The system namespace path also fails: get_system_extattr(&name) gets ENOATTR, and fill_system_extattrs treats that as 'removed since the listing' and drops the attribute. Stock rustic calls xattr::list, which gives the exact OsString bytes, so its value read succeeds; this is a regression in fork code (fork code, not upstream, so rule 3 does not cover it). restic-bko's nodeFillExtendedAttributes calls getxattr with the exact Go string bytes, so it gets the value; the two forks lose node parity, which is a rule 4 concern and supports the finding. Non-UTF-8 names are real input: any user can make one with setextattr. The result is silent loss of a value, which matches S1 ('wrong result on real input'). Two names that convert to the same lossy string also collide in BTreeMap/node names. The fix keeps output where names are valid UTF-8, so rule 5 does not win: the output changes only in the broken case.

column4: 3 checklist 3 (errors carry what failed; nothing lost silently); API Guidelines C-GOOD-ERR
column6: fill_acls uses the file's shared `unsupported` predicate (lines 181-186), which counts EPERM and EACCES as 'no ACL'. An ACL the backup user may not read is dropped with only a debug line.
column7: FreeBSD ZFS, backup run as a non-root user, a file whose NFSv4 ACL lets that user read_data but not read_acl. OpenZFS zfs_getacl checks ACE_READ_ACL and returns EACCES (from memory of OpenZFS; not checked against source here). get_acl fails with EACCES, `unsupported` says true, and the node is stored with no ACL and no warning. The restore then gives the file a trivial ACL from its mode. EPERM and EACCES belong in that predicate only for the system-extattr listing (the 'not root' case at line 298).
column8: Split the predicate: use EOPNOTSUPP/EINVAL for ACL reads, and keep EPERM/EACCES only for listing the system namespace. Report an ACL that can't be read the way mapper.rs reports an unreadable xattr (a warning), rather than as a hard error that fails the node.
column9: confirmed: Confirmed from the code. freebsd_netbsd.rs:181-186 `unsupported` matches EOPNOTSUPP|EINVAL|EPERM|EACCES, and fill_acls (line 334) uses it for get_acl, so an EACCES from __acl_get_link becomes a debug line and the node is stored with no ACL. The EACCES case is real: OpenZFS zfs_getacl checks ACE_READ_ACL through zfs_zaccess, and UFS NFSv4 getacl checks VREAD_ACL. A non-root user who can read a file but not its ACL hits it, and the ACL is lost silently (checklist 3). The restic fork's attrs_bsd.go:108 has the same predicate, so the fix should go into both. It only adds a warning and leaves nodes unchanged, so node parity (rule 4) holds. Rule 5 covers holt output only, and this is our own file, not upstream, so no rule wins.

column4: 6 checklist 6 (duplication between modules); Effective Rust (one implementation per behaviour)
column6: FreeBSD's restore_symlink_mode re-implements osattrs::chmod_symlink through its own hand-declared lchmod (lines 46-48), with a different error policy.
column7: chmod_symlink (osattrs.rs:1670, used on NetBSD/OpenBSD/DragonFly) treats EOPNOTSUPP/EINVAL, 'a file system that keeps none', as a debug line. FreeBSD's copy turns every lchmod failure into a path_error. So when lchmod(2) refuses with EOPNOTSUPP/EINVAL, FreeBSD reports one error per restored symlink where the other BSDs report none. Which FreeBSD file systems refuse this way is not verified here. FreeBSD also has fchmodat(AT_SYMLINK_NOFOLLOW), so the extra extern block is not needed.
column8: Add target_os = "freebsd" to chmod_symlink's cfg, make freebsd::restore_symlink_mode call it, and delete the lchmod extern block.
column9: confirmed: The duplication is real. freebsd.rs:291-301 restates chmod_symlink (osattrs.rs:1669-1688) through its own lchmod extern (lines 46-48), and the error policy differs: chmod_symlink sends EOPNOTSUPP/EINVAL to the debug log, while FreeBSD's copy turns every failure into a path_error. One correction to the stated failure: restore.rs:1743 warns and calls tally.count. restore_error_counts does not count an EOPNOTSUPP failure (ErrorKind::Unsupported), so FreeBSD prints a warning per symlink rather than a counted error. An EINVAL failure would be counted. Which FreeBSD file systems refuse this way is still unverified, but duplicated logic with a different policy is S2 under RA5 on its own. The code is ours, so no rule wins.

column4: 7 checklist 7/1; the Rustonomicon and std docs: every unsafe fn has a # Safety section
column6: netbsd_sys::{acl_get_link, acl_set_link, lpathconf} are `unsafe fn` with no `# Safety` section. Their SAFETY comments say only 'for which the caller vouches', without saying what the caller must vouch for.
column7: Not a runtime failure. A maintainer adding a caller can't tell from the code that `path` must be a NUL-terminated C string, `acl` must point to a writable, fully initialised struct acl with acl_maxcnt == ACL_MAX_ENTRIES, and acl_cnt must be <= 254 for set.
column8: Add `/// # Safety` with those obligations to each of the three functions. Better still, make them safe wrappers that take &CStr and &mut RawAcl, so that only the syscall line is unsafe.
column9: confirmed: freebsd_netbsd.rs:91-112 has three `pub(super) unsafe fn` (acl_get_link, acl_set_link, lpathconf) with no `# Safety` section. Their inner SAFETY comments only say 'for which the caller vouches'. The bar requires `# Safety` on every unsafe fn, and RA5 lists a missing `# Safety` as S2. clippy::missing_safety_doc doesn't fire on non-pub items, so no lint will catch it. The file is ours, so no rule wins.

column4: 1 checklist 1 (FFI constants checked against the platform headers, file and version cited)
column6: NetBSD's ACL syscalls are made by raw number (487, 488, 499), and the _PC_ACL_EXTENDED/_PC_ACL_NFS4 values (14, 17; freebsd_acl.rs:99-100) are hard-coded. Neither names the NetBSD release they come from, and I could not check them against a header (none is on this Mac).
column7: If a NetBSD release ever numbers these differently, syscall(487, path, type, acl) becomes some other syscall called with pointer arguments: undefined behaviour, or ACLs silently missing. That is conditional, and today's numbers are unverified rather than known to be wrong. The tests pin the values but don't prove them.
column8: On the NetBSD guest, check sys/sys/syscall.h and sys/sys/unistd.h (NetBSD 10.x) and cite the file and release in the comments. If NetBSD's libc exports `__acl_get_link`/`__acl_set_link`/`lpathconf` (check with `nm -D /usr/lib/libc.so`), link them by name as freebsd_sys does and drop libc::syscall.
column9: downgraded: The citation really is missing: neither file names the NetBSD release or header the numbers come from. The failure case is not real, though. NetBSD keeps syscall numbers stable as ABI and adds compat entries rather than renumbering. The numbers are also proven on a real system, not merely pinned: testvm/compare/netbsd/roundtrip.sh sets POSIX.1e and NFSv4 ACLs on FFSv2ea vnd images on netbsd11 (11.1), including symlink ACLs via setfacl -h. It compares getfacl output after the restore (check 'ACLs (netbsd.acl_*)'), and wrong syscall or pathconf numbers would make that check fail. The restic fork pins the same 487/488/499. What is left is citing the header and release in a comment, which is doc polish: S3.

column4: 7 checklist 1/7 (cite header file and version)
column6: The FFI layouts and constants cite headers without an OS version: struct acl (here), the flag bits (bsd_flags.rs:6, 68), the ACL tags and perms (freebsd_acl.rs:18-55), and _PC_* (freebsd_acl.rs:88-89). ZfsXattr and its ioctls (freebsd.rs:63-83) cite truss on FreeBSD 15.1, not OpenZFS's header.
column8: Name the header and release on each block, e.g. 'FreeBSD 15.0 sys/sys/acl.h', and for ZfsXattr OpenZFS's header that defines zfsxattr_t. column4: 2 Checklist 2 (no panic or wrong result reachable from input such as file names); Book ch. 9 (bad input is not trusted); the fork's own restore.rs:716 already refuses node paths that would leave the destination
column6: set_xattrs and restore_one_xattr_meta pass a snapshot's xattr name straight to openat/fchownat/fchmodat/utimensat relative to the attribute directory, and on illumos '..' in an attribute directory is the file itself (fsattr(7)), so a name like '..' or '../x' reaches the file or the real tree outside the attribute space.
column7: A snapshot (crafted, or from a damaged repository) holds a regular-file node /r/f with extended_attributes [{name: "..", value: "X"}]. At restore, attr_names leaves out '.' and '..', so '..' counts as missing, and open_attr(dir, "..", O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_TRUNC) opens /r/f itself and truncates it: the restored data becomes "X". If xattr_meta has an entry for '..', restore_one_xattr_meta then fchownat/fchmodat's the base file to that entry's uid and mode (0o4755 owned by 0, say). A directory node /r/d with the name "../../../etc/x" makes root create /etc/x (mode 0600, the attacker's value) outside the restore target. A name "SUNWattr_rw" writes the system-attribute view. Linux, the BSDs and Haiku never resolve xattr names as paths, so only illumos is exposed. Checked by reading the code and fsattr(7); not run on a guest.
column8: Add a valid_attr_name(name) check, used by set_xattrs (before the open and the 'present' check) and by restore_one_xattr_meta. It refuses an empty name, '.', '..', any name containing '/' or NUL, and the SYSTEM_VIEWS names, and pushes an InvalidData error for that name to XattrErrors (or returns it as the first failure). Test: in illumos.rs tests, set_xattrs(file, [xattr("..", b"X")]) is Err and the file's contents are unchanged; set_xattrs(dir, [xattr("../x", b"y")]) is Err and dir/x does not exist.
column9: confirmed: The code path is real and nothing validates the name on it. LocalDestination::set_extended_attributes (illumos cfg) goes to osattrs::set_native_xattrs, then osattrs.rs:1440 os::set_xattrs, then illumos.rs:776 set_xattrs. That function hands the snapshot's a.name to open_attr, which does openat(attrdirfd, name, O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_TRUNC, 0600). restore_one_xattr_meta (illumos.rs:941) hands the same name to fchownat, fchmodat, openat and utimensat relative to the attribute directory. Neither function checks for '.', '..', '/', or the SYSTEM_VIEWS names. attr_names (703) leaves out '.' and '..', so a '..' entry never counts as present and always reaches the O_TRUNC open. On illumos/Solaris, '..' in an attribute directory is the base file (fsattr; runat ls -la shows '..' as the file itself). So '..' truncates the restored file and writes the attacker's value into it, and an xattr_meta entry for '..' chowns and chmods the base file. Through a directory node, '../...' resolves into the ordinary tree, so root can create files outside the restore target. That is the same escape the fork already refuses for node paths at restore.rs:716 (target_of). A real Linux snapshot can't produce such a name, because Linux names carry a namespace prefix. So the input is a crafted snapshot written by a repository key holder, such as another host sharing the repo. A damaged repository would fail the MAC instead. The restic fork's xattr_illumos.go has the same unvalidated openat, which suggests the hole was carried over. No rule wins: illumos.rs is a fork-owned file (rule 3 doesn't apply), and refusing these names keeps repositories readable (rule 4). Rule 5 means the fix changes behaviour and goes to the user, but the finding stands. Caveats: this is from reading the code and illumos semantics, not a run on a guest. That multi-component '../x' crosses out of the attribute namespace is the least certain part; the single '..' truncation alone justifies S1.

column4: 1 Checklist 1 (no UB on any target the cfgs admit); Rustonomicon on references and raw pointers; std's own unix readdir (library/std/src/sys/fs/unix.rs) uses ptr::addr_of!/offset_of for d_name for exactly this reason
column6: CStr::from_ptr((*e).d_name.as_ptr()) makes a &[c_char] of libc's declared d_name length, which is 3 on illumos (libc 0.2.189 src/unix/solarish/mod.rs), then reads the whole name through a pointer derived from that 3-byte reference.
column7: Any extended attribute whose name is 3 bytes or longer, which is nearly every one ("user.comment", say): xattrs_read -> attr_names reads past the bounds of the 3-byte reference. Under Stacked Borrows (Miri) that is UB. It works today only because rustc does not exploit it.
column8: Take the name without a reference: let name_ptr = unsafe { ptr::addr_of!((*e).d_name) }.cast::<c_char>(); then CStr::from_ptr(name_ptr). Put both in one SAFETY comment saying the kernel NUL-terminates d_name inside the record. No test can run Miri on illumos; the cross-target clippy run plus the existing set_xattrs_leaves_equal_ones test on the guest cover the change.
column9: confirmed: Confirmed from the code. Line 702 of crates/core/src/backend/osattrs/illumos.rs (branch backotter of rustic_core, one of our own added files, so rule 3 does not exempt it) reads `CStr::from_ptr((*e).d_name.as_ptr())`. Cargo.lock pins libc 0.2.189, and that version's src/unix/solarish/mod.rs declares `d_name: [c_char; 3]`. Calling `.as_ptr()` on the array autorefs it to a 3-element reference, so the pointer CStr::from_ptr walks along is derived from a 3-byte borrow. Any name of 3 bytes or more (every real xattr, read through xattrs_read -> attr_names) is then read out of that borrow's bounds, which Stacked Borrows treats as UB. std's own unix readdir (library/std/src/sys/fs/unix.rs) explains this hazard for dirent's trailing d_name and uses `&raw const (*entry_ptr).d_name` to avoid it, which matches the finding's cited source. None of our rules wins: the fix is a hunk in our own file and changes no output (changes_output false is right). The rust-audit.md definition puts unsound code at S1, so the severity stands. The proposed fix, `ptr::addr_of!((*e).d_name).cast::<c_char>()` (or `&raw const`), matches std.

column4: 1 Checklist 1; Rustonomicon (a reference must be dereferenceable for its whole size); std's unix readdir comment on the 'imaginary' size of d_name
column6: The same (*e).d_name.as_ptr() pattern on Haiku makes a &[c_char; 1024] (libc 0.2.189 haiku/mod.rs declares d_name as [c_char; 1024]; Haiku's <dirent.h> has a flexible char d_name[]), which asserts 1024 bytes are dereferenceable past the entry.
column7: fs_read_attr_dir is readdir() on a DIR that Haiku mallocs at DIR_BUFFER_SIZE 4096 bytes and fills with packed entries, returning first_entry + next_entry (src/system/libroot/posix/dirent.cpp, master). An entry that starts more than about 3,050 bytes into that buffer gets a 1024-byte reference running past the end of the allocation, which is UB. It is unverified whether any Haiku file system returns more than one attribute entry per read; BFS appears to return one. If none does, this stays latent, hence S2 and not S1.
column8: As in illumos.rs: ptr::addr_of!((*e).d_name).cast::<c_char>() and then CStr::from_ptr, with the SAFETY comment updated. The existing Haiku-guest tests (files_dirs_and_symlinks_keep_their_own and others) cover it.
column9: confirmed: rustic_core backotter haiku.rs:117 does CStr::from_ptr((*e).d_name.as_ptr()). That autorefs the whole d_name field, and libc 0.2.189 (Cargo.lock) declares it on Haiku as [c_char; 1024], so the code makes a 1024-byte reference over an entry whose name is really a flexible array. Haiku's readdir packs entries into a 4096-byte malloc'd DIR buffer and hands out first_entry + next_entry, so the reference can run past the allocation, which is UB. Whether that ever happens depends on a file system returning more than one attribute entry per _kern_read_dir. BFS returns one, and the code doesn't show any that returns more, so this is latent and S2 is right rather than S1. The fix (addr_of!(...).cast()) is local to our own osattrs file, so no rule wins. I could not open the libc source locally; the 1024 declaration is from the finding and known libc.

column4: 3 Checklist 3 (errors are not lost); C-GOOD-ERR; readdir(3C): NULL is both the end and an error, told apart only by errno. haiku.rs:100-113 already does this correctly.
column6: attr_names treats every NULL from readdir as the end of the attribute directory, so a read error silently cuts the listing short.
column7: readdir fails partway through an attribute directory (EIO on a damaged pool, say, or EOVERFLOW). Three things follow. xattrs_read returns Ok with only the names before the error, so the backup drops the rest of the file's xattrs with no warning. fill_xattr_meta drops their metadata. On an in-place restore, set_xattrs sees a short 'present' list and fails to remove stale attributes, which breaks exactness, again with no error.
column8: Set errno to 0 before each readdir (illumos: *libc::___errno() = 0) and, on NULL, return io::Error::last_os_error() when it is nonzero, as haiku.rs's set_errno loop does. Close the DIR on both paths. Test: none can inject a readdir error portably; factor the loop into a helper that takes a readdir closure and unit-test its errno handling.
column9: confirmed: illumos.rs attr_names breaks on any NULL from readdir without clearing or checking errno, so a mid-listing read error gives a short Ok list. xattrs_read then drops the remaining attributes without a warning, and set_xattrs works from a short 'present' list and leaves stale attributes behind. haiku.rs's set_errno loop already does this correctly. restic-bko's attrNames (xattr_illumos.go) uses Readdirnames(-1) and returns the error, so fixing this brings rustic-bko into line with restic-bko instead of breaking parity. It is an error-handling defect, so S2.

column4: 3 Checklist 3 and 5 (errors say what failed; no lossy round trip); haiku.rs/haiku_attrs.rs keep names as bytes and warn about non-UTF-8 ones
column6: attr_names converts names with to_string_lossy and later opens or unlinks by the lossy string, so a non-UTF-8 attribute name gets a misleading ENOENT, and an in-place restore cannot remove it.
column7: A file has an attribute named b"caf\xe9" (Latin-1). In xattrs_read, open_attr("caf\u{fffd}") gives ENOENT, so the backup warns that the attribute is unreadable with 'No such file or directory' rather than 'name isn't UTF-8'. In set_xattrs on an in-place restore, the lossy name is not in attrs, unlinkat("caf\u{fffd}") fails with ENOENT, the restore reports 'removing caf\u{fffd}: No such file', and the real attribute stays.
column8: Have attr_names return Vec<Vec<u8>> (or OsString). Callers skip non-UTF-8 names with an explicit warning, as haiku.rs kept() does. set_xattrs unlinks by the original bytes when a name is not wanted. Test: on the guest, an attribute with a non-UTF-8 name is reported with the explicit warning, and an in-place set_xattrs(&[]) removes it.
column9: confirmed: attr_names returns to_string_lossy names, and xattrs_read and set_xattrs then call open_attr and unlinkat with CString::new(lossy name). For a non-UTF-8 name that gives ENOENT: the backup reports the attribute as unreadable with a misleading 'No such file', and an in-place restore fails to remove the real attribute and reports an error naming the replacement-character string. haiku_attrs.rs keeps names as bytes and reports non-UTF-8 ones separately, and restic-bko's Go code opens and unlinks by the raw bytes, so this is a rustic-bko-only divergence. A warning message changes, so the user must approve it (rule 5 routes it, it doesn't drop it). Such names are rare, so S2 holds.

column4: 2 Checklist 2 (no resource exhaustion reachable from on-disk input); Effective Rust (bounded allocation on input)
column6: attr_value reads each illumos extended attribute whole into memory with read_to_end, and haiku_attrs::read_attr allocates fs_stat_attr's size + 1 (haiku_attrs.rs:129); on both systems an attribute is effectively a file of any size, and its value then goes inline into the tree JSON.
column7: On illumos, `runat f cp /big.iso iso` gives f a 4 GiB named attribute. A backup of f allocates 4 GiB for the value, then base64-encodes it into the node, about 5.4 GiB in the tree blob. The likely result is an OOM kill of the whole backup, or else a giant tree blob. On Haiku, a BFS attribute stored in its own inode can be just as large.
column8: Cap the size, checked before reading (st_size from fstatat, attr_info.size), at a limit that matches restic-bko's. An attribute over the cap goes to XattrsRead::unreadable (Haiku: an error for that name, the others kept) with a 'too large to keep (N bytes)' message. This changes what a backup keeps, so the user decides first (rule 5). Test: a FakeBfs attribute of cap + 1 bytes is refused without being read; an illumos-guest test creates a large attribute file and checks it is listed as unreadable.
column9: confirmed: The code matches the finding. illumos attr_value reads the whole attribute with read_to_end, and haiku_attrs::read_attr allocates vec![0; size + 1] from fs_stat_attr with no cap. A named attribute on illumos is an ordinary file of any size: runat, or an SMB alternate data stream stored as a named attribute. So a large one makes the backup allocate it whole and inline it, base64-encoded, into the tree JSON. One correction to the fix: restic-bko has no cap to match. Its getxattr in xattr_illumos.go is a plain io.ReadAll. Any limit is therefore a new behaviour change in both forks, which keeps node parity (rule 4), and it is the user's decision (rule 5). No rule makes the finding moot, and as unbounded allocation from on-disk input it fits S2.

column7: --delete restore. A later name `b` of a hard-linked file is in the destination and has other names outside it. Its node sets flags (immutable). clear_restricting_flags_held takes the flag off, remove_file(b) fails (say EPERM from an append-only parent whose node doesn't set flags), and held.put_back() also fails. Result: only `debug!("... not removed early")`. The file's other names stay without the immutable flag, and nothing is counted or warned. The metadata pass's own remove_held clears nothing (the flag is already off), so it can't report this either.
column8: Match `(Err(err), put_back)` and, besides the debug line, call `put_back_failed(&target, &perr)` when put_back is Err, as remove_in_the_way does.
column9: confirmed: At backotter 695d676, restore.rs 1203-1206 is `match remove_held(&target, true, ...)`, and its `(Err(err), _)` arm discards the put-back result, logging only at debug. Every other remove_held caller (684, 751-759, 1075, 1538) reports a failed put-back whether or not the removal worked. HeldFlags::put_back (osattrs.rs 503) can return Err: the ioctl or fchflags fails, or a file cleared by path is gone. If that happens, the flags stay off the old inode. The metadata pass can't report it later: link_name's own remove_held finds nothing left to clear, so its put-back succeeds. Then the late pass sets flags on the canonical inode linked over the target, not on the old one. The fix makes the call site report what the others already report. It needs both the removal and the put-back to fail, so it is rare, but it is a lost error, which is S2. No rule of ours wins: rule 5 covers style fixes, and this is a real error path in the fork, not a holt output.

column9: confirmed: longpath.rs:35 is `imp::shorten(path).map_or(Cow::Borrowed(path), Cow::Owned)`, so every io::Error from shorten, link_to (symlink) and make_dir (ENOENT/EACCES from DirBuilder::create, or the AlreadyExists after 1000 names) is dropped. It is not rule-wins: this is our own file, so rule 3's out-of-scope does not apply, and the fix adds a message, so rule 5 sends it to the user rather than dropping it. changes_output=true is right.

column7: --strict-exit with a [repository] run-before hook that takes a few seconds, and Ctrl-C at the terminal while it runs. SIGINT reaches the hook child (same process group), which dies, so run_before returns Err. Meanwhile the interrupt thread has set INTERRUPTED and is running the global failed hooks. The main thread then goes into the Err arm and runs the repository's run-failed and run-finally hooks (hooks.rs:133-136), which the docs say never run after an interrupt. If run_before returns Ok instead (a SIGTERM the hook didn't see), f runs: for restore, forget, prune and so on there is no nested use_with to stop it, so the command starts while the failed hooks run (backup alone is stopped, by its source-level use_with).
column8: Take the result of run_before, call crate::application::halt_if_interrupted(), then match it: `let before = self.run_before(); crate::application::halt_if_interrupted(); match before { ... }`. Test: make the halt decision a pure function (for example `fn interrupted() -> bool` that halt_if_interrupted uses) and unit-test use_with's ordering with a hook stub. As written, the parking loop can't be tested directly.
column9: confirmed: use_with (rustic src/config/hooks.rs:109-140 on backotter) calls halt_if_interrupted() only on entry and after f(). Nothing checks between run_before returning and either the Err arm (run_failed + run_finally at :133-136) or the call to f. The SIGTERM case doesn't even depend on timing. ctrlc is built with the "termination" feature (Cargo.toml:109), so a `kill` sent only to rustic doesn't reach the hook child. The interrupt thread (commands.rs:206-211 -> application.rs:71-81) sets INTERRUPTED and runs the global failed/finally hooks while the run-before hook carries on. When that hook returns Ok, f runs with no check: for repository.rs:72 run_indexed that means restore, forget, prune and the rest, until process::exit. The SIGINT/Err case is a real race. Both contradict the doc comment at hooks.rs:106-108 and rustic BACKOTTER.md:275-277. None of our rules wins: rule 5 only sends the behaviour change to the user and does not drop the finding. The fix narrows the window but does not close it: a hook list in run_all can still go on to its next command after an interrupt.

Weak parts: docs/design/reformat.md's row scopes it to 'a btrfs whose dump has grub_env_block', so code and doc agree (item 7 weak, item 3 carries it); a block without the signature at dump time was already broken on the source; the same old dump without --reformat (commands.rs:2462) is 79ff930's gap, not this unit's. S2 as filed, like H7-08, H7-14, R4-04: only dumps from before 79ff930 on three distros with --reformat.

They differ only in how lsinitrd names the image (`-k KVER` vs `IMAGE`), the kernel loop, and how dracut gets the image and kver.
column7: The rule 'keep what the restored image had' lives in two hand-copied sh strings with nothing tying them together, so the next fix to one silently skips the other: a module-compression suffix the `\.ko[.a-z0-9]*` regex misses, a change to dracut's 'dracut modules:' header, or the mktemp leak (`{ f=$(mktemp) && printf ... > "$f"; } || exit` exits without removing $f when the write fails). Fixed in DRACUT_EACH_KERNEL only, Gentoo's copy stays broken and Gentoo loses modules or resume again, the hibernation regression a41658d fixed. Each constant's test (dracut_keeps_the_restored_images_modules, dracut_one_image_keeps_modules_and_resume) checks only its own string.

column6: 695d676 makes the walk reach directories past PATH_MAX, but the ignore crate (0.4.33, not vendored) still reads ignore files by their long path: dir.rs:1039 `if cfg!(windows) || gipath.exists()` (exists() is false on ENAMETOOLONG) and dir.rs:350 `dir.join(".git").metadata().ok()`. So with --git-ignore or --custom-ignorefile, a .gitignore, custom ignore file or .git whose path is PATH_MAX bytes or more is skipped without a warning, and the files it excludes go into the snapshot.
column7: Back up /src with `--custom-ignorefile .rusticignore`, where /src/<120 x 40-byte dirs>/.rusticignore holds `secret.key` and secret.key sits next to it (about 4.9 KB, like fail-001's tree). Walk::next calls ig.add_child(ent.path()), add_child_path(dir, None), create_gitignore; gipath.exists() fails with ENAMETOOLONG, the rule is never loaded, and secret.key is backed up with no warning, so --strict-exit doesn't catch it. Before 695d676 the subtree was left out with a warning. BACKOTTER.md says ignore files past PATH_MAX 'fail as before', but nothing fails. Same for --git-ignore: a .gitignore past PATH_MAX, or a repo whose .git is past it (with require_git its rules aren't applied).
column8: The ignore crate is upstream, so fix it in our code: when git_ignore is set or custom_ignorefiles is non-empty, check each directory whose path plus the longest ignore-file name is PATH_MAX bytes or more for those names through walkdir::short_path; if one exists, warn naming the long path and count it in Incomplete so --strict-exit fails (a fuller fix reads and applies it). Correct BACKOTTER.md's 'fails as before'. Test: test_backup_past_path_max_ignorefile, a custom ignore file 4.9 KB deep, expecting a warning and a non-zero strict exit (or the file excluded).
column9: CONFIRMED: at 695d676 LocalSource::new sets git_ignore, git_exclude, require_git and add_custom_ignore_filename on ignore's WalkBuilder; Cargo.lock pins ignore 0.4.33 from crates.io, only walkdir is patched, and that walkdir lists and lstats through short_path, so the walk now enters those directories. ignore-0.4.33's sequential Walk (walk.rs ~1239-1243) calls add_child(ent.path()) -> add_child_path_with_found_ignore_files(dir, None) -> create_gitignore, whose `gipath.exists()` (dir.rs:1039) reads ENAMETOOLONG as 'not there' and pushes no error; dir.rs:350 misses a deep .git the same way. Nothing warns or counts in Incomplete. 695d676 turned a reported omission into a silent wrong result. No rule wins: rule 3 keeps the ignore crate out of scope but the fix is in our code; rule 5 is about style fixes. BACKOTTER.md's 'where a long path fails as before' is wrong for ignore files. S2 not S1: the limit is documented, the input is contrived, and the error backs up more rather than losing data.

column6: Several functions replace their `path` argument with the short path before they warn or build an error, so messages name a path inside $TMPDIR/.bko-longpath-PID-N/, removed at exit, instead of the file's own path: osattrs::fill's 'ignoring file flags/attributes of {path}', keep_unread, the debug in clear_restricting_flags, map_path (mapper.rs:113 passes the short path: 'ignoring extended attribute {name} of {path}', ErrorLink/ErrorXattr { path }), remove_held (restore.rs:2289) through remove_tree's 'N entries not removed, the first {path}', exact::clone_file (exact.rs:218: '{src} isn't N bytes', TempLeft's 'temporary file {tmp} is left behind'). BACKOTTER.md says every message keeps the long path except errors from LocalDestination's own calls, so it is wrong as well.
column7: A non-root restore with --delete into a destination holding a 0555 directory D at a 4.9 KB-deep path with a file inside, where the snapshot has a regular file named D: remove_in_the_way calls remove_held, which shortens D and calls remove_tree(short); remove_file fails with EACCES and the error logged is '1 entries not removed, the first /tmp/.bko-longpath-4242-0/1/d061.../D/f: Permission denied', a path gone once the process exits. Likewise a failed --exact reflink clone that can't remove its temporary file reports it by a /tmp link path, and a backup warning about an unreadable xattr on a deep file names the /tmp path.
column8: Keep the caller's path for messages and use the short one only for the system calls: in the osattrs wrappers bind `let sys = walkdir::short_path(path);` and pass &sys to os::*; give map_path the long path (shorten inside the calls); format remove_held and clone_file errors with the original paths. Update BACKOTTER.md's sentence on messages. Test: a deep removal that fails, asserting the message holds the long path and not '.bko-longpath'.
column9: CONFIRMED: read at 695d676. osattrs.rs:134 fill rebinds `let path = &*walkdir::short_path(path);` before its 'ignoring file flags/attributes of' warnings; keep_unread (~274) and clear_restricting_flags' debug! use the rebound path; mapper.rs:113 calls map_path(&walkdir::short_path(entry.path()), ..), whose warn and ErrorLink/ErrorXattr take the short path; restore.rs:2289 remove_held shadows target before remove, so remove_tree walks WalkDir::new(short) and its 'entries not removed, the first' names the link path (the outer error! names the long one, the inner text the short one); exact.rs:218 clone_file shadows (src, dst), so CloneFailed::TempLeft's tmp is under the short dst. BACKOTTER.md and the commit message promise the long path except for sys_path errors, so item 7 fails too. No rule wins (our own lines; rule 5 sends the output change to the user, it doesn't drop the finding). S2 not S1: only paths of PATH_MAX bytes or more, the short path keeps the real tail, no data or exit status is wrong.

column4: 3 Checklist 3 (no lost source: errors carry what failed); std Error/C-GOOD-ERR
column6: short_path throws away the io::Error from imp::shorten (`map_or(Cow::Borrowed(path), Cow::Owned)`) and returns the long path. The system call then fails with ENAMETOOLONG and the real cause is never shown: $TMPDIR missing or read-only, $TMPDIR longer than 1024 bytes, symlink() failing with ENOSPC or EROFS, or a component too long to cut.
column7: `TMPDIR=/nonexistent rustic backup /deep` with 4.9 KB paths, or a restore from a rescue system with a read-only /tmp: make_dir fails with ENOENT or EROFS, short_path returns the long path, and every entry past PATH_MAX warns 'File name too long' and is left out, the very symptom 695d676 was written to fix, with nothing pointing at TMPDIR. make_dir is also retried on every long path, because a failure is not remembered.
column8: Keep short_path's signature for walkdir's callers, but also report the failure: remember the first shorten error in a OnceLock and expose it (or a `try_short_path(&Path) -> io::Result<Cow<Path>>`), so rustic_core can warn once (walkdir has no log dependency), e.g. 'paths past PATH_MAX can't be reached: no link directory in $TMPDIR: <err>'. Document it. Test: with TMPDIR at a missing directory, in a child process (DIR is process-wide), try_short_path returns the error.
column9: CONFIRMED: at 695d676 longpath.rs:35 (54 at today's head) drops every error from shorten, including make_dir, symlink and current_dir. Each listed cause is real: DirBuilder.create gives ENOENT/EROFS, a $TMPDIR over CHUNK/2 = 1024 gives too_long(), symlink errors pass up by `?` in link_to, an uncuttable component gives too_long(). DIR is set only on success, so make_dir is retried per path. About 60 callers in crates/core (osattrs, ignore, mapper, local_destination sys_path, restore, exact) get a Cow and can't see the error, so the call fails with the same ENAMETOOLONG 695d676 meant to fix: a lost source (item 3, C-GOOD-ERR). It already cost us: 81ed0b5 says symlink() failed with ENAMETOOLONG on an XFS $TMPDIR (1024-byte link targets), so .16-.18 still left long paths out, hidden behind this map_or for three releases. No rule wins: longpath.rs is our file, the fix keeps short_path's signature; a new warning is a behaviour change, so RA7 not RA6. S2 not S1: no new wrong result, the entries still fail with warnings and strict-exit is unchanged.

column6: A link's path is temp_dir() joined as given, so if $TMPDIR has a symlink component every round's link path holds it. Resolving a k-round short path then follows 2k links, not k, and the reach is halved. The module doc ('Other links along the path (in $TMPDIR, say) count toward the 40 too') and BACKOTTER.md read as a one-time cost.
column7: TMPDIR=/scratch/tmp where /scratch is a symlink to /data: each L_i is /scratch/tmp/.bko-longpath-PID-0/i and its target starts with L_{i-1}'s spelling, again through /scratch, so resolving L_k/rest follows two links per round and ELOOP comes at about 20 rounds. With 40-byte names a path of about 42 KB (2048 chunk) or 22 KB (1000 chunk) fails with 'Too many levels of symbolic links' and the backup leaves it out; the docs promise about 82 KB and 42 KB. (Kernels before 4.2 capped nested follows at 8, and each round nests one deeper.)
column8: In make_dir use std::fs::canonicalize(std::env::temp_dir()) (falling back to the plain path on error) and apply the TMP_MAX check to the canonical path, so no link path contains a symlink. In both docs say symlinks in the original path's first prefix count once and the links' directory is canonical. Test: TMPDIR a symlink to a real directory, in a child process, reaches a path of about 25 rounds (stat succeeds).
column9: CONFIRMED, and tested on Chopin (kernel 7.2.12): a chain of links whose targets each go through the link before, as short_path's do, stats fine at depths 18-30 under a canonical directory, but under a directory reached through one symlink depth 19 is OK and 20 onwards fail with 'Too many levels of symbolic links'. So reach halves (about 20 rounds, ~41 KB with 2048-byte chunks, ~21 KB with 1000, against the docs' 82/42 KB); with s symlinks in $TMPDIR it is 40/(1+s) rounds. Realistic: on ostree systems /home links to var/home, so a TMPDIR under $HOME has one. The module doc (31-32) and BACKOTTER.md's 'Depth limit' read as a one-time cost (item 7). No rule wins (our file, stock-tool compatibility untouched, no holt output). S2 not S1: deeper paths fail with a clear ELOOP and are left out, which the design accepts past its limit.

column6: long_paths_reach_the_same_file expects LONG whenever a 1025-byte target is taken, while probe asks for a 2048-byte target. Any file system whose limit falls between them makes the test fail although the code is right. The docs name only XFS and 1 KiB-block ext2/3/4/minix as SHORT cases.
column7: $TMPDIR on ext4 (or ext2/3) made with -b 2048, limit 2047 bytes: probe's 2048-byte symlink gets ENAMETOOLONG, so chunk = SHORT, which is correct; takes_long_targets() makes a 1025-byte link, which succeeds, so long_ok = true, and `assert_eq!(chunk, if long_ok { LONG } else { SHORT })` fails: a false failure in the vendored walkdir's tests.
column8: Have takes_long_targets make a target of imp::LONG bytes (the same test as probe, read back whole), or reuse probe against a second independent probe. Add ext2/3/4 on 2 KiB blocks (limit 2047) to the SHORT cases in the module and SHORT docs.
column9: CONFIRMED: read at a5785e7; the kernel's limits settle it. probe (186-200) makes a LONG = 2048-byte target and picks SHORT if that fails; takes_long_targets (312-317) makes a 1025-byte one; the test (356-358) asserts chunk == if long_ok { LONG } else { SHORT }. ext4's fscrypt_prepare_symlink(dir, symname, len, s_blocksize, ..) refuses len + 1 > block size, and ext2's check is the same, so 2 KiB blocks give 2047: probe rightly returns SHORT, the 1025-byte link succeeds, and the assert fails. The test asks a different question than the code (item 8) on any limit between 1025 and 2047. The module doc (16-19), SHORT's doc (78-81), probe's doc (181-185) and BACKOTTER.md (267-277) miss the 2 KiB ext case (item 7). No rule applies (our file). S2 not S1: probe chooses correctly, so no backup or restore is wrong; only a false test failure (fork-tests.sh would report it fork-only) and an incomplete doc. Not S3: no lint names it.

column6: Since .19 a temporary directory of 501-1024 bytes gets no links at all, even where probe would choose LONG. .16-.18 served these, and the per-round shortening argument holds for LONG up to about 1740 bytes. The bound SHORT / 2 is applied before the chunk is known.
column7: TMPDIR is a 700-byte path on tmpfs or 4 KiB-block ext4: make_dir returns ENAMETOOLONG, for_process fails, and every path at PATH_MAX or longer comes back as-is; the backup leaves it out ('File name too long', exit 3) and the restore can't make it. Under .18 the same machine reached those paths with 2048-byte prefixes.
column8: In make_dir check against LONG / 2 (1024, as in .18); in for_process, after probe, if chunk == SHORT and the directory path is longer than SHORT / 2, remove the directory and return too_long() (or keep the bound per chunk with a const assert for each). Update the short_path doc and BACKOTTER.md ('one of over 500 bytes'). Test: Links::with_chunk with a 700-byte dir and LONG shortens a 330-deep path.
column9: CONFIRMED: at f2428c3 (.18) make_dir refused a TMPDIR only past CHUNK / 2 = 1024 (longpath.rs:117) with 2048-byte prefixes; at a5785e7 it refuses one past TMP_MAX = SHORT / 2 = 500 (88, 209) before probe runs, so also on tmpfs, btrfs or 4 KiB ext4 where probe returns LONG, and for_process fails into the old ENAMETOOLONG. A link's path is TMPDIR plus ~30 bytes and a LONG round's cut lands past 2048 - 256, so shortening holds up to ~1,750 bytes; the const assert TMP_MAX + 50 < SHORT - 255 only has to bind for SHORT. So 501-1024-byte TMPDIRs worked in .16-.18 and fail since .19, and .20 brought back the 2048-byte prefixes without this range. No rule wins (our file; a bound plus a post-probe check changes no output, it only serves paths refused today). S2 not S1: the failure is graceful (stock rustic's 'File name too long'), documented ('one of over 500 bytes'), and such TMPDIRs are rare (the farm's are short); on par with R8-02. Not S3: no lint names it.

column4: 3 checklist 3/7 (the module doc promises the directory is 'removed at exit'); std::process::exit docs (other threads keep running while exit handlers run)
column6: The atexit handler remove_dir doesn't take LINKS. A worker thread still inside Links::shorten can make a link while remove_dir_all runs; the rmdir then fails with ENOTEMPTY and the 0700 directory of links to the user's directories stays in $TMPDIR.
column7: A restore's rayon workers call short_path on deep paths while the main thread calls std::process::exit (an error exit in rustic): remove_dir_all unlinks 0..n, a worker's symlink creates n+1, rmdir fails, and $TMPDIR/.bko-longpath-PID-0 with link n+1 is left behind.
column8: In remove_dir take LINKS with `lock().unwrap_or_else(PoisonError::into_inner)` and set a closed state (a `closed: bool` in Links, or an AtomicBool checked in shorten under the lock) before remove_dir_all, so later calls return too_long(). Hard to test deterministically; cover with a comment.
